articles.title: Nashville fans lay flowers and light candles in tribute to Dolly Parton
articles.summary: The BBC's Helena Humphrey is outside the Country Music Hall of Fame where fans gathered to mourn Dolly Parton.
articles.body:
The BBC's Helena Humphrey visited the Country Music Hall of Fame in Nashville, Tennessee, on Tuesday evening as fans gathered to mourn Dolly Parton. The country music star died at the age 80 after a brief battle with cancer, her team announced.

Nashville You are now following Nashville Updates from your News topics will appear in My News and in a collection on the News homepage .

articles.title: Starving on the front lines: Food supply in crisis as Ukraine fights Russia
articles.summary: Photos of emaciated Ukrainians reveal conditions suffered by Ukraine, as meagre rations also afflict Russian soldiers.
articles.body:
Kyiv, Ukraine – Pleas and photos of four emaciated soldiers roiled Ukraine in late April.

The group had reportedly been starving on the front line after up to 17 days without food deliveries and months without rotation.

list 1 of 4 ‘Ukraine has momentum in war with Russia’

list 2 of 4 Putin hints at ending Russia’s war in Ukraine, but why now?

list 3 of 4 Russia kills three Ukrainians in 24 hours, accuses Kyiv of violating truce

list 4 of 4 Russia and Ukraine accuse the other of ceasefire violations

“Fighters faint because of starvation, they drink rainwater,” Anastasia Silchuk, whose husband serves in the 14th Mechanised Brigade, said on social media on April 22.

The fighters were holed up on the left, eastern bank of the Oskil River in the southeastern Donetsk region after Russian bombs destroyed the bridges connecting them to their brigade on the right bank.

“They weren’t listened to on the radio, or perhaps no one wanted to listen to them. My husband shouted and begged, saying there was no food and water,” Silchuk wrote.

She did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for an interview.

Oleksandr, a soldier who has served recently, told Al Jazeera that he has felt the effects of extreme hunger while fighting for his homeland.

While holed up in an isolated, scrupulously hidden bunker on the treeless, open front lines of southeastern Ukraine earlier this year, Oleksandr missed his family, home and the life he had before Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion. But what he missed the most was real food.

“You dream of a hot meal, because what you get for weeks is chocolate bars, oatmeal and a bottle of water a day,” the serviceman recovering from a leg wound in Kyiv, told Al Jazeera.

The gaunt, tattooed 31-year-old, who is getting used to a ceramic kneecap, withheld his last name and details of his service in accordance with wartime protocol.

Quantum leaps in the evolution of military drones hovering 24/7 above the kill zone that now extends up to 25km (15.5 miles) from both sides of the front line have made interconnected, walkable trenches or supply vehicles nearly obsolete.

The technological and tactical breakthroughs turn positions on the Ukrainian side into isolated, island-like spots, and the supply of food, ammunition, medication and even power generators becomes a new matter of life or death.

“Gone are the days when you could just come out of a bunker to have a smoke,” Ihor, who commands a drone unit in eastern Ukraine, told Al Jazeera.

Things on the Russian side are also dangerous, as soldiers are ordered to move in twos or threes to bypass Ukrainians and amass manpower and ammunition for minor breakthroughs.

But they are often hunted down by drones.

Small, inexpensive and explosives-laden suicide drones have made tanks and armoured vehicles look like dinosaurs that are about to go extinct.

The only vehicle that can escape a suicide drone is a four-wheel drive darting and zigzagging forward at 120km/h (75mph), but few risk driving one across rugged terrain covered with explosion craters and landmines.

“Once, we lost four pickups in one day,” Oleksandr said.

Robotised carts on wheels with video cameras can deliver ammunition and food to front-line outposts and drive back wounded soldiers.

But they still need light reconnaissance drones to guide them. Heavier drones – mostly bombers that can release their cargo of several kilograms and fly away – are often the only lifeline.

For at least a year, front-line logistics has been mostly handled with drones or robotised carts, according to Andriy Pronin, one of Ukraine’s drone warfare pioneers.

For the most part, the new supply system works smoothly.

“All of my friends [on the front line] get everything on time, once a day, once every other day, everything according to the schedule,” Pronin told Al Jazeera.

Nikolay Mitrokhin, a researcher with Germany’s Bremen University who monitors and analyses the ongoing war, doubts the scope of drone supplies.

“No more than 10 percent of the entire [Ukrainian] army” gets drone-dropped food, Mitrokhin told Al Jazeera.

A disrupted drone supply could lead to cases of starvation.

Days after the images of emaciated soldiers went viral, the brigade’s officers said in a statement that “delivery of everything, from a piece of bread to a disassembled generator … is carried out by air” and Russian forces “intercept, shoot down as many drones as possible”.

The brigade’s commanding officer was, however, fired.

The Defence Ministry ordered an investigation and said on April 28 that insufficient food supply to the brigade and two more military units nearby “must not become systemic”.

Oleksandr said he remembers a time when drones were a novelty to Russian soldiers.

“When we flew the heavy Vampire drones, they would look at them above them until they dropped their load,” Oleksandr said. “And then some would fall, and some would flee. Or crawl away.”

In March 2025, a bit of drone-dropped food smoothed a soldier’s surrender.

The Third Stormtrooper Brigade spotted a starving Russian soldier who was hiding in the snow-swept forest in the northeastern Kharkiv region. Having witnessed the deaths of fellow servicemen, he signalled with signs to a Ukrainian reconnaissance drone that he would give himself up. He did so after receiving a chocolate bar with instructions on how to get to Ukrainian positions written on it.

Soldiers on the Russian side are often sent on high-risk missions with next to no drone-dropped food.

“They gave me a small bottle of water, two or three very small chocolate bars,” Mohammad, a Tajik labour migrant duped into “volunteering” to fight against Ukraine, told Al Jazeera in September 2025.

He said he spent almost a month in an abandoned village in the eastern Luhansk region. With scarce drone deliveries, he searched for raw macaroni and food scraps.

Mohammad said his weight before the war was 76kg, and even after several weeks of three meals a day at a Ukrainian detention centre for prisoners of war, he still weighed 60kg.

In October 2025, Ukrainian intelligence claimed that hundreds, if not thousands, of Russian soldiers were abandoned on the islands of the Dnipro River between Russia-occupied and Ukrainian-controlled parts of the southern Kherson region and had “serious problems” with food and ammunition supply.

There have been reported, unverified cases of cannibalism among starving Russian servicemen.

In late April, British daily The Times cited an intercepted conversation of two Russian officers talking about a soldier who had killed a fellow serviceman, “cut off a leg” and was about to eat it, but was shot dead by another serviceman.

articles.title: Zelenskyy asks Putin for meeting: What’s he offering, could Russia accept?
articles.summary: Russia and Ukraine have been holding peace talks since the war began in 2022, but with no concrete outcome.
articles.body:
Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has written an open letter to Russia’s President Vladimir Putin and proposed a meeting to discuss ending Moscow’s four-year war on Kyiv.

The letter, which was published in full on the Ukrainian president’s website on Thursday and sent via diplomatic channels to Russia as well as countries including the United States, comes as Russia’s war on Ukraine continues to rage into its fifth year.

list 1 of 3 Could Russia hit northern Europe if it gained control of Arctic’s Bear Gap?

list 2 of 3 Russia launches massive overnight attack on Ukraine

list 3 of 3 Ukraine drone attack kills 8 in Russian-held territory in new escalation

On Thursday, at least 12 people were killed and dozens injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine, according to Ukrainian authorities. Zelenskyy also commemorated at least 707 children killed by Russian attacks during the two countries’ more than four-year-long war.

Meanwhile, in Russian-occupied Ukraine, at least four people were killed in Ukrainian drone attacks on Thursday. Ukraine also struck an oil complex and naval base in St Petersburg, Russia, on Wednesday.

Russia and Ukraine have been holding indirect peace talks since the war began in February 2022, but with little or no concrete outcomes. US President Donald Trump has also met both Putin and Zelenskyy, seeking to bring them to the negotiating table to discuss ending the war, but so far, his efforts have not borne fruit.

Will Zelenskyy’s open letter to Putin open a new path to a ceasefire?

In his letter, Zelenskyy told Putin that he has spent nearly half of his 26 years in power in Russia “waging war against Ukraine” and said Russians are now growing increasingly tired of Ukrainian missiles and drone attacks, inflation and fuel shortages.

“We can all see that Russians are finally becoming less comfortable with this reality – with the fact that the war is bringing more and more negative consequences to Russia,” he wrote.

He also told Putin that a prolonged war could threaten the Russian president’s personal position. “It is a fact of Russian history that you know well: When Russia grows tired, change comes,” he said.

“After 26 years in power, age is beginning to take its toll. And with time, the fatigue with you will only grow,” he added.

Zelenskyy also wrote that while he and the Ukrainian people are less concerned about the loss of Russian lives on the battlefield, every loss of a Ukrainian counts. “Even when the ratio of Ukrainian losses to Russian losses is one to five or one to six, it still matters greatly.

“We in Ukraine do not want a permanent war. We know very well that life without war is infinitely better. And we want to achieve that,” he said.

Zelenskyy noted that with the US focused on its war on Iran, “it would be wrong to simply wait until the war in Europe returns to the centre of its attention,” and suggested a path to peace.

“Do not be afraid to take the path out of this war. That is the main thing that is required of you now.

“Ukraine proposes ending this war through direct engagement between us – and you. I am proposing a meeting… If you do not personally come to the conclusion that it is time to end this war, Ukraine will continue fighting for its existence,” he added.

Regarding the location of the meeting, Zelenskyy said: “There are countries that have traditionally hosted leaders to resolve issues of war and peace. Switzerland, Turkiye, the countries of the Arab world – many are able and willing to host such a meeting.

“We believe Europe should be part of this process – those who truly have the capacity to influence the situation. We also believe that the United States must be part of the process. This is what could help shape a new security architecture for our part of the world,” he added.

Writing on X, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha described the letter as “a serious and meaningful proposal to end the war … with clear, doable steps and an invitation for a personal meeting”.

“We expect a meaningful response to this proposal. It’s time to end this war. It’s time to choose peace.”

Markus Ziener, a senior visiting fellow at the German Marshall Fund of the United States Berlin office, told Al Jazeera that making the letter public forces Russia to openly show its hand while proving to the world that Ukraine is ready for diplomacy.

“It places the moral high ground and the pressure to respond entirely on the Kremlin,” he said.

He noted, however, that this is not the first time Zelenskyy has reached out to Putin.

“Most recently on May 11, 2025, he publicly and explicitly announced that he was ready to travel to Turkey to meet Putin in person for face-to-face talks,” he said.

Zelenskyy’s new proposal shows that the Ukrainian president “feels emboldened by the successful military pushbacks against the Russian army on the battlefield, including successfully targeting Russian infrastructure far in Russian mainland”, Ziener said.

“The Ukrainian president believes that, currently, the momentum is on his side and therefore it is good moment [to] offering talks.”

Has Putin accepted Zelenskyy’s proposal?

The Russian president’s spokesman told reporters in Russia that Putin was aware of Zelenskyy’s letter but had not yet been briefed about its content in detail.

But at Russia’s showcase annual economic forum in St Petersburg on Thursday, Putin said his troops were continuing to advance in Ukraine.

“The offensive is ongoing on a daily basis. At present, the Russian Federation has taken full control of the Luhansk People’s Republic – 100 percent. And Russia has brought more than 85 percent of the territory of the Donetsk People’s Republic under its control. (And) 80 percent of the territory of the Zaporizhzhia region,” he said, referring to three of the four regions in Ukraine which Moscow has claimed as its own since 2022.

“Naturally, under these circumstances, the Ukrainian side would like us to halt the advance. But rather than stopping that, it would be better to bring the war to an end altogether by agreeing to the compromises that were discussed in Anchorage,” he said, referring to a summit he held in Alaska with Trump, which ended without any agreement, in August 2025.

In his letter to Putin, Zelenksyy wrote that Ukraine had heard that Russia “promised in Alaska the resolution of certain issues concerning Ukraine and Europe”, but added that issues on Ukraine and Europe could not be decided in Anchorage.

“Since the war is taking place in Europe, and since Ukraine needs security guarantees, while you [Putin] also seek security guarantees for yourself, it would be logical to involve those who can genuinely serve as guarantors,” Zelenskyy said.

While it is unknown if Putin will accept Zelenskyy’s proposal, he told the conference in St Petersburg: “We are certainly prepared and willing to reach an agreement with Ukraine through peaceful means. Specifically, on the basis we discussed during our meeting with President Trump in Anchorage.

“As for what we might say to one another if we were to reach the end of the conflict, at the very least we could – and indeed should say, ‘Thank goodness it’s all over,'” he added.

So far, Putin has only agreed to meet Zelenskyy in Moscow or a third country, once a peace agreement is finalised.

Ziener said it is highly unlikely that Putin will agree to Zelenskyy’s latest proposal while Russia is militarily under pressure, as agreeing to direct talks could be seen as a weakness on the part of the Kremlin.

“Furthermore, meeting Zelenskyy as an equal would undermine years of Kremlin propaganda aimed at delegitimising the Ukrainian president,” he said.

Will the US and Europe play a bigger role now?

Since Trump became president of the US for the second time in January 2025, he has been promising to end Russia’s war in Ukraine.

He has met both Russia’s President Putin and Ukraine’s President Zelenskyy in separate meetings to discuss ending the war, but so far, these efforts have not borne fruit.

Truce talks have largely stalled due to Russia’s insistence on keeping territory it has seized from Ukraine. Ukraine has stated that it is not prepared to cede any territory.

On May 22, US State Secretary Marco Rubio said that while trilateral talks had been unsuccessful, the US was ready to organise a new round of peace talks.

Zeiner noted that while Trump is signalling support for the initiative by Zelenskyy, a key question remains on whether that actually means there will be US support for Ukraine.

“Of course Trump wants the war to end. But he is so consumed by the war with Iran that he may not be willing to engage more in Ukraine. Europe definitely supports Zelenskyy’s move,” he said.

European leaders, who have been largely sidelined in peace talks since Trump returned to the US presidency last year, have repeatedly called for ceasefire talks between Russia and Ukraine since the war began in 2022.

In May this year, the leaders of the United Kingdom, France, Germany and Poland met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for talks in Kyiv, in a show of unity a day after Russia’s Vladimir Putin hosted his allies at a Victory Day parade in Red Square.

On Wednesday, a German official told the Reuters news agency that a window for dialogue is slowly opening between Russia and Europe on Ukraine, although it is likely to be months before talks could ‌begin.

While it is unclear who will lead these talks, the German official told Reuters there are strong indications that Germany, France and the UK will play an important role.

On Thursday, Putin rejected European leaders’ involvement in truce talks.

“How can the EU or individual EU countries serve as mediators when they are directly assisting the country with which we are in an armed conflict?” he questioned journalists in St Petersburg.

“Mediation implies neutrality,” he added.

articles.title: Torfaen becomes global hotspot for carbon emissions after wildfires
articles.summary: The smell of burning from the Blaenavon wildfire was reported 30 miles away in Cardiff.
articles.body:
A county in Wales had one of the world's highest carbon emissions per square kilometre due to wildfires in July, according to a charity.

The fire above Blaenavon, Torfaen was described as "one of the largest and most challenging" in south Wales in recent years by the fire service.

Save the Children said it was concerned about possible health consequences after data , external published by the European Union's earth observation programme, Copernicus, showed Torfaen behind Malanje in Angola, Spain's Ãvila and Annaba in Algeria in terms of wildfire emissions in July.

Torfaen council said it was unaware of the EU data but its own air quality monitoring showed "elevated particulate concentrations".

A blaze the size of about 300 football pitches broke out on Mynydd Garnclochdy, between Abersychan and Blaenavon, with people reporting smelling smoke about 30 (48km) miles away in Cardiff.

Combined with others across the region it contributed to a major incident being declared , which eventually required assistance from the military .

Blaenavon councillor Janet Jones said the smoke had been "particularly bad" on 13 August - about three weeks after the fire first ignited.

"There was great concern about air quality and the impact on elderly people and those suffering with respiratory issues such as emphysema and COPD."

Jones said she had spoken with GP practice nurses two weeks ago and was not aware of any increase in patients complaining about respiratory problems, but added this "could change in the months ahead".

Melanie Simmonds, head of Save the Children Wales, said: "In Wales and across the world, children are breathing in smoke from wildfires, coping with extreme heat and losing the freedom to play outdoors because the air is no longer safe.

"These conditions are not only frightening - they carry serious health consequences for children whose bodies and lungs are still developing."

Torfaen council said it was not aware of the research and "it is not clear what data or evidence was used in the assessment to arrive at the reported conclusion".

It said it "recognises that prolonged wildfire incidents have the potential to adversely affect local air quality, particularly through increased levels of smoke and particulate matter".

It added it "continuously monitors" air quality through a monitoring station in Croesyceiliog Cwmbran.

"While elevated particulate concentrations have been observed during the wildfire period, the council's monitoring station is intended to provide information on general background air quality rather than conditions at specific locations immediately adjacent to the fires," it said.

The Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) website , external said it was part of European Union's Space programme, and provided global information related to air pollution and health.

Its data said emissions in Torfaen had been "extremely unusual".

articles.title: Cancer patient campaigns to scrap VAT on sunscreen
articles.summary: The 26-year-old says she wants the tax gone to make sunscreen "more accessible to more people".
articles.body:
A Sussex woman is calling on the government to scrap VAT on sunscreen after being diagnosed with skin cancer at the age of 26.

Jessica Zbinden-Webster from Ferring in West Sussex will deliver a petition of almost 100,000 signatures to Downing Street, calling on the government to scrap the 20% VAT charged on sunscreen products.

Diagnosed in 2018 Zbinden-Webster said she wanted the government to axe the tax to make sunscreen "more accessible to more people".

The government says it will "fight cancer on all fronts".

Describing her treatment Zbinden-Webster said the tumour had spread quite deep underneath the surface of her skin.

"So I had that lopped off and then the hole was so big that it couldn't be closed with stitches.

I was warned, you know, you may look a little different for a while and as you can see from the pictures, I did look a little different for a while."

Determined to raise awareness of the disease she says it affects about 20% of the population, but it is avoidable in nine out of 10 cases.

"In a cost-of-living crisis, the poorest are priced out of skin cancer prevention because of the 20% 'cosmetic' tax on sunscreen products. Sunscreen is not 'cosmetic' - it's critical," she said.

Zbinden-Webster's says the petition is highlighting that skin cancer is now the most common form of cancer in the UK.

A government spokesperson said: "As part of our 10-year plan to reform the health service, and through a national cancer plan, we will fight cancer on all fronts, from prevention, to diagnosis, treatment, and research.

"High-factor sunscreen is on the NHS prescription list for certain conditions and is already provided VAT free when dispensed by a pharmacist to these patients."

articles.title: Always tired? Leaving your ‘loops’ open may be the unexpected cause
articles.summary: Procrastinating on some tasks may feel harmless, but the perpetual mental hum of unfinished business may cause more stress than you realize.
articles.body:
The texts you've ignored, the vacation supplies you still need to order, the hard conversation you've been avoiding — repeatedly putting off such tasks because they feel too daunting may seem relatively harmless. But the constant mental hum of unfinished business may be more draining than you realize — like your laptop slowing and glitching because you have 90 browser tabs open.

Some people are waking up to that reality, sharing on social media and in podcasts their epiphanies about the countless open "loops" in their lives in need of closing. The buzzy phrase helps them more easily recognize and combat the habit.

As New Yorker Florence Friebe learned about open loops, she began to see the pattern in her own life — for example, via a hole in her jacket pocket that she kept neglecting to fix and remembered every time she dropped her keys or phone into it.

"I could really start seeing how many repetitive thoughts I was carrying, and how much space it was taking," added Friebe, cohost of the podcast "2 Curly Haired Girls With ADHD" — referring not only to the effects of procrastinating on fixing her jacket pocket but also on cleaning and work tasks.

Psychologists who study procrastination say these people are right to address these issues.

The inertia comes from perceiving "the 'cost' of doing the task in terms of time, energy, and emotional fatigue," said Dr. Vara Saripalli, a clinical psychologist in private practice in Chicago, via email. "They aren't thinking about the other negatives that ensue from waiting; they're focused on the present and avoiding unpleasantness in the here and now."

But as Friebe learned, avoidance also can be highly costly, both practically and by taking up energy that could be used for other things, Saripalli added.

Procrastination and chronic stress can eventually take a toll on both your mental and physical health, said Dr. Fuschia Sirois, professor of social and health psychology at Durham University in England. Sirois, a procrastination expert who has been studying the issue for 25 years, is also the author of "Procrastination: What It Is, Why It's a Problem, and What You Can Do About It."

Those impacts include causing or contributing to a weakened immune system, chronic disease, anxiety and digestive issues, low self-esteem and loneliness, Sirois added.

For Lanna, a content creator and Pilates instructor in Germany, procrastination-related worries even caused stomachaches, she said. Lanna requested that CNN use her nickname for privacy.

But for many people, awareness of these impacts doesn't always make taking action easier.

For generally healthy people, habitual procrastination typically boils down to two causes, even if the details differ per individual, experts said: negative emotions associated with certain tasks or with the prospect of those tasks not going well.

Maybe you're delaying replying to a text because you haven't figured out a perfect response, and you have complicated feelings around imperfection. Or maybe you're avoiding a serious talk with a friend because you're people-pleasing or worried you'll be hurt. (You can read more about procrastination "styles" and related tips here .)

Procrastinating on relatively minor things sometimes may stem from a broader societal shift Saripalli has noticed, in which people are less comfortable with finality and losing options, she said. "The simple task of returning a package becomes an internal monologue of, 'What if I change my mind and I can't get this item again? I'm better off holding on to it till I'm sure.'"

On the other hand, you may just have too many responsibilities and need to consider which ones you can forgo. Maybe you're exhausted by other commitments or spending too much time on your phone, which can be a distraction and energy zapper.

Or maybe the cause of your procrastination is more complicated. If you're struggling to overcome procrastination on your own, consider seeing a doctor or therapist to determine whether there's a more serious underlying issue, Sirois said — such as depression, ADHD or an anxiety disorder.

These disorders can make one's tolerance of negative feelings about a task much lower, Sirois added. That, as well as other symptoms, can contribute to people with these disorders being more prone to procrastinate.

In those cases, some coping strategies can help, but they don't cure disorders or replace professional assistance, Sirois said.

That was true for Lanna, who said she has ADHD and autism, and for Friebe. Friebe said she realized that her struggles with procrastination were significantly tied to her ADHD, depression and polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome , or PMOS.

"It was almost like I was lacking ingredients," Friebe said. "Once I got diagnosed, it felt like a giant relief."

Awareness of your urges to procrastinate and of the likely consequences can sometimes be enough to help you regulate your emotions, then choose differently.

But some people such as Friebe and Lanna have also sought professional help for their conditions and improved their lifestyle habits. These changes have given them more energy and the confidence to be more efficient.

Seeing a therapist can really be helpful for anyone regardless of whether you have a condition since they can help you deal with pessimistic ideas causing procrastination. Sirois recently released a free, online evidence-based tool kit for that purpose.

Now Friebe schedules free time to tackle whatever tasks she's got at the moment. Doing a job little by little — or styling to-do list tasks that way — has been more effective than anticipating it with the all-or-nothing thinking that can make responsibilities feel daunting. What also helps Lanna is doing activities that rejuvenate her.

And Friebe really means little , even if that feels stupid, she said. She referred to a story she heard of people who wanted to start exercising at a gym driving to the gym, as they were, on the days they had said they wanted to work out — but not going inside.

The next time, those people also put on workout clothes before driving. Next, they went to the gym in their outfits and exercised for only five minutes. "What they were actually building was trust that they were reliable, that they could do it, so then it could accumulate," Friebe said. "Before you knew it, they were working out."

Studies support the effectiveness of such gradual habit-building.

Guilt and shame are the two most common emotions people feel when they procrastinate, Sirois said, which compound the problem and further paralyze you — even though taking action would alleviate all those negative feelings. "Being self-compassionate is actually a more effective way to get oneself back on track," she added.

Acknowledge that you're struggling and what you're feeling, and ask yourself whether the situation at hand will really be that bad. "Often, we anticipate things are going to be much worse than what they are," Sirois said. Even if your attempts don't go well, trust that you can learn how to navigate the fallout and be OK.

Also try to find the meaning in different responsibilities, those interviewed recommended. If you're delaying cleaning your room and beating yourself up about whether your roommate is judging you for the mess, think about the fact that you deserve a clean, cozy space.

Friebe and Lanna consider how productivity might bring them closer to their life purpose or the person they want to be. And if a heart-to-heart goes poorly, even then, the meaning can be that you grew in your ability to handle conflict, and that you have the truth about the relationship and can act accordingly.

If you're avoiding scheduling a doctor's appointment because you don't want to hear their feedback, your health issue exists regardless. So why not get some answers and prevent your problem from worsening? Regardless of the task, think of how relaxed you'll feel and how much time you'll free up for other fun things if you just get it done.

Since Friebe has improved her health and learned what strategies work for her, "the way I speak to myself is completely different," she said.

"I have a better sense of self and identity and self-trust," Friebe added. "My entire life has changed. I'm a different person."

Get inspired by a weekly roundup on living well, made simple. Sign up for CNN's Life, But Better newsletter for information and tools designed to improve your well-being.

For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com

articles.title: What should you wear through airport security? Frequent fliers recommend these fuss-free pieces
articles.summary: Consider this your cheat sheet for a smoother trip through TSA lines — not to mention a smoother trip overall.
articles.body:
Our experts independently review everything we recommend. If you buy through our links, we may earn commission.

Getting through airport security is stressful enough, so your outfit shouldn't be the thing holding up the line. Looking polished is always a plus, but the best travel outfits work smarter, not harder. Think easy-on, easy-off shoes , layers that don't require a full wardrobe change and clever pieces that keep you from frantically digging through your bag while everyone behind you silently judges.

So, what actually deserves a spot in your airport uniform? We asked frequent fliers to share their wardrobe standbys. From shoes made for breezing through security to fuss-free layers and smart, travel-friendly details, consider this your boarding pass for getting through the airport with less hassle — and more time for the important things, like finding your gate and grabbing a snack (or maybe a pre-flight glass of wine).

These things don't have to be on opposite sides of the terminal. The best travel outfits hit that sweet spot: Soft, stretchy and roomy enough to survive hours in a cramped seat, but polished enough that you won't be rushing to change the second you land. "I think comfort and style go hand in hand," says travel YouTuber Ally Gibson . "Comfort is non-negotiable, especially on long-haul flights. That said, you never know who you might meet, and looking good makes you feel good throughout the day."

Sometimes the secret to a comfortable travel outfit is less what you wear and more what you leave at home. "I avoid jeans, belts and anything tight because sitting in restrictive clothing becomes uncomfortable on a long travel day, especially when your body can feel more swollen during a flight," explains travel blogger Hazel McKinlay .

And while the days of dressing formally for a flight may be long gone, that doesn't mean airport style has to look like pajamas. "Comfort is definitely No. 1 for me, but I still want to look nice!" says Megan Miele, account manager of business travel at Cadence Travel . "My mom was a flight attendant and started flying back in 1969. Back then, you dressed up to the nines to get on an airplane. Flying was more of a privilege and was much more exclusive than it is today.

"Now, almost everyone can afford to fly, and we fly a LOT more often. We also have so many more rules and regulations to deal with. So for me, comfort is definitely the priority, but I still want to feel like I look put together. I'm not trying to show up at the airport looking like I just rolled out of bed," she added.

The modern-day happy medium? Start with pieces you can comfortably sit, stand and sprint to your gate in, then lean on a few smart styling tricks to make your travel look more polished. Layer a chic, cozy sweater over a soft T-shirt and leggings for an easy upgrade, or take the guesswork out of getting dressed with a cute matching set .

Colorfulkoala High-Waisted Tummy-Control Leggings

The best airport outfits include pieces that work smarter, not harder, especially when you're juggling a suitcase, a boarding pass and an overpriced airport coffee. "Layers are useful because airport and aircraft temperatures can vary so much. In colder weather I always take a scarf, which earns its place in my hand luggage several times over: I wear it at the airport and then use it as a blanket, wrap or makeshift pillow on the plane," says McKinlay.

Andrés Serra, trip planner and head of operations at Optimise Travel , has his travel-day formula down to a science. "My favorite travel outfit is a plain T-shirt, elastic-waist travel pants with two zipped pockets, a thin button-up overshirt and low-profile sneakers. The overshirt acts as a light jacket and can be rolled up to support my neck if I need it, and the pants are comfortable for long flights but still look good enough for a restaurant after landing." Cara Laban, founder of TravelReddi , agrees that pockets are a travel-day must. "I recommend pants with large pockets so you can easily grab essentials like your ID or passport and phone without having to dig through your bag," she says.

Choosing travel pieces that pull double duty doesn't just make the journey more comfortable — it also frees up precious space in your suitcase . A button-up can double as a pillow, an oversized scarf becomes an in-flight blanket and a pair of polished pants can hold your essentials and take you straight from a cramped coach seat to dinner without an outfit change. The more versatile each piece is, the less you have to pack.

And don't forget about what's underneath your outfit. Gibson recommends compression socks for long travel days, calling them "a game-changer for leg fatigue and circulation." They may not be the star of your airport look, but your legs could be thanking you by the time you land.

What items help you breeze through airport security?

A little pre-security prep can mean the difference between an easy trip through the checkpoint and becoming that person frantically scooping up loose change and jewelry while the line piles up behind you. "The most useful thing I bring isn't something I wear," says Serra. "It's a small zipped pouch I keep in my personal bag. Before I leave for the airport, I put my watch, coins, wallet, earbuds and other small items inside. TSA suggests putting pocket items in your carry-on instead of leaving valuables loose in a screening tray. This also saves me from scrambling to grab everything while other people are waiting."

Your bag can also do some of the heavy lifting. "If you are traveling with a laptop or iPad, a bag with a separate laptop compartment will make it much easier to get it in and out at security," explains Laban. She also recommends skipping jewelry and belts loaded with metal, since they can add another thing to remove — and another thing to remember on the other side.

And don't forget the right shoes. "If you don't have TSA PreCheck (which I highly recommend), then slip-on shoes, or just shoes that don't have difficult laces, are definitely helpful," Laban adds.

Gibson swears by a crossbody with plenty of pockets, like her go-to Bandolier bag . "It keeps my phone, ID, passport, wallet, headphones and lip gloss within reach. There's even a dedicated front phone pocket, which makes keeping track of everything at security a breeze." Everything should have a designated spot, so you can spend less time digging through your bag at security and more time relaxing in the airport lounge.

And while the days of dressing formally for a flight may be long gone, that doesn't mean airport style has to look like pajamas. "Comfort is definitely No. 1 for me, but I still want to look nice!" says Megan Miele, account manager of business travel at Cadence Travel . "My mom was a flight attendant and started flying back in 1969. Back then, you dressed up to the nines to get on an airplane. Flying was more of a privilege and was much more exclusive than it is today.

"Now, almost everyone can afford to fly, and we fly a LOT more often. We also have so many more rules and regulations to deal with. So for me, comfort is definitely the priority, but I still want to feel like I look put together. I'm not trying to show up at the airport looking like I just rolled out of bed," she added.

The modern-day happy medium? Start with pieces you can comfortably sit, stand and sprint to your gate in, then lean on a few smart styling tricks to make your travel look more polished. Layer a chic, cozy sweater over a soft T-shirt and leggings for an easy upgrade, or take the guesswork out of getting dressed with a cute matching set .
Colorfulkoala High-Waisted Tummy-Control Leggings

The best airport outfits include pieces that work smarter, not harder, especially when you're juggling a suitcase, a boarding pass and an overpriced airport coffee. "Layers are useful because airport and aircraft temperatures can vary so much. In colder weather I always take a scarf, which earns its place in my hand luggage several times over: I wear it at the airport and then use it as a blanket, wrap or makeshift pillow on the plane," says McKinlay.

Andrés Serra, trip planner and head of operations at Optimise Travel , has his travel-day formula down to a science. "My favorite travel outfit is a plain T-shirt, elastic-waist travel pants with two zipped pockets, a thin button-up overshirt and low-profile sneakers. The overshirt acts as a light jacket and can be rolled up to support my neck if I need it, and the pants are comfortable for long flights but still look good enough for a restaurant after landing." Cara Laban, founder of TravelReddi , agrees that pockets are a travel-day must. "I recommend pants with large pockets so you can easily grab essentials like your ID or passport and phone without having to dig through your bag," she says.

Choosing travel pieces that pull double duty doesn't just make the journey more comfortable — it also frees up precious space in your suitcase . A button-up can double as a pillow, an oversized scarf becomes an in-flight blanket and a pair of polished pants can hold your essentials and take you straight from a cramped coach seat to dinner without an outfit change. The more versatile each piece is, the less you have to pack.

And don't forget about what's underneath your outfit. Gibson recommends compression socks for long travel days, calling them "a game-changer for leg fatigue and circulation." They may not be the star of your airport look, but your legs could be thanking you by the time you land.
What items help you breeze through airport security?

A little pre-security prep can mean the difference between an easy trip through the checkpoint and becoming that person frantically scooping up loose change and jewelry while the line piles up behind you. "The most useful thing I bring isn't something I wear," says Serra. "It's a small zipped pouch I keep in my personal bag. Before I leave for the airport, I put my watch, coins, wallet, earbuds and other small items inside. TSA suggests putting pocket items in your carry-on instead of leaving valuables loose in a screening tray. This also saves me from scrambling to grab everything while other people are waiting."

Your bag can also do some of the heavy lifting. "If you are traveling with a laptop or iPad, a bag with a separate laptop compartment will make it much easier to get it in and out at security," explains Laban. She also recommends skipping jewelry and belts loaded with metal, since they can add another thing to remove — and another thing to remember on the other side.
And don't forget the right shoes. "If you don't have TSA PreCheck (which I highly recommend), then slip-on shoes, or just shoes that don't have difficult laces, are definitely helpful," Laban adds.

Gibson swears by a crossbody with plenty of pockets, like her go-to Bandolier bag . "It keeps my phone, ID, passport, wallet, headphones and lip gloss within reach. There's even a dedicated front phone pocket, which makes keeping track of everything at security a breeze." Everything should have a designated spot, so you can spend less time digging through your bag at security and more time relaxing in the airport lounge.

articles.title: UnitedHealth Stock's Biggest Risk Sits In The Commercial Book
articles.summary: Medicare's improvement is real but not a turn in cost trend, while commercial costs keep running higher and the margin fix there has slipped again.
articles.body:
Medicare's improvement is real but not a turn in cost trend, while commercial costs keep running higher and the margin fix there has slipped again.

UnitedHealth (UNH) shares are up about 34% over the past year, ahead of the S&P 500's 21%, on a recovery in margins the company is only partway through. Two of the moving parts in that recovery are pulling in opposite directions, and the one that is deteriorating has no date on its fix.

Year-over-year revenue growth, after topping 12% for two straight quarters, has stepped down over the last two periods to 2.0% and now 0.4%, and the company has intentionally prioritized margin discipline over top-line volume. UnitedHealthcare expects full-year 2026 Medicare Advantage enrollment to decline by approximately 1.1 million through benefit adjustments and selective changes in market participation aimed at margin stability. On $450.1 billion of trailing-twelve-month revenue, that is a business trading size for profitability, and with the top line flat every dollar of earnings recovery now has to come out of cost.

Medicare Is Improving Without The Trend Inflecting

Medicare is where the repair is working . Management expects the 2026 Medicare medical cost trend to come in below its initial estimate of around 10%, pointing first to its own benefit design, care management models and network curation. Management also names a more favorable respiratory season and weather patterns alongside them. The company-wide reported second-quarter medical care ratio of 86.7% was itself helped by $860 million of net favorable prior period medical development, the majority of which was in-year development. Management is explicit that the softer Medicare trend is not an inflection point.

An Ineffective Arbitration Process Is Adding Cost

The commercial side is going the other way. Commercial medical cost trend is running modestly above the 11% the company had been seeing. The independent resolution process under the No Surprises Act, which applies only to commercial plans, is adding 50 basis points or so of incremental trend in 2026 and now totals at least 100 basis points of cost. The company's management characterizes the process as inefficient, noting that dispute filings are heavily concentrated among a small number of provider groups. Add provider coding intensity in office visits and emergency departments, and full commercial margin recovery has been pushed past 2027 . Margin repair on a timetable that keeps moving is a different proposition from the strong margins the Trefis High Quality Portfolio looks for in its holdings.

articles.title: What credit score is needed to refinance your mortgage?
articles.summary: If you have bad credit, you need to find ways to compensate for the additional risk.
articles.body:
A credit score of at least 620 will qualify you for a conventional refinance — but clearing the minimum doesn't guarantee a good rate. Lenders save their best pricing for borrowers well above the cutoff, and the difference can add up to real money over the life of the loan.

Minimums vary by loan type: 580 for FHA, generally 700+ for jumbo, and no set agency floor for VA or USDA (though lenders typically look for 620 and 640 respectively). A score that rules out one option may still work for another.

If your score is borderline, run the math on closing costs vs. savings before you refinance — sometimes it's cheaper to spend a few months improving your score first.

If your score is well below your loan type's minimum, refinancing may not be your best move right now. A repayment plan or loan modification through your current servicer can offer payment relief without locking you into a new rate for years.

Meeting the minimum credit score for your loan type is only step one. Lenders price loans on a sliding scale, so qualifying and getting the best available rate are two different things — and the gap between a borderline score and a strong one can cost you real money over the life of the loan. Some low-score borrowers can benefit from government-backed streamline refinances, which forgo the credit check altogether.

Keep in mind that if your new rate isn't a real improvement over your current one, refinancing may actually cost you more than it saves once you factor in closing costs. Taking the time to improve your credit score can unlock access to a lower rate when you apply.

Read on for the minimum score you'll need by loan type and how to decide whether refinancing with bad credit — or not refinancing at all — is the right call.

What credit score is needed to refinance a house?

No credit minimum from VA, but lenders generally require 620

No credit minimum from USDA, but lenders generally require 640

These numbers are guidelines. The credit score you need to refinance depends on your lender, your individual situation and the type of refinance you choose. For example, lenders tend to have more stringent requirements for a cash-out refi than a traditional rate-and-term refinance.

You might also find that your lender wants a higher score if other parts of your financial picture aren't as strong, for instance, if you have a high debt-to-income (DTI) ratio .

articles.title: 9 commons myths about wrinkles debunked — and what dermatologists want you to know instead
articles.summary: From the importance of genetics to whether $200 moisturizers are a good buy, here's the whole truth and nothing but the truth.
articles.body:
Our experts independently review everything we recommend. If you buy through our links, we may earn commission.

I once read about a lady who didn't smile for over 40 years . Her reason for such a stationary expression was not a distaste for joy and laughter, but something else entirely — to prevent wrinkles . She'd decided that maintaining a straight, expressionless face was worth it to keep smooth, youthful-looking skin. (Apparently, she even resisted smiling when her daughter was born! Can you imagine?)

Sometimes, when I'm slathering on my lotions and potions in the evening, I think about this woman. Not because it's a cautionary tale about vanity, but because her fear wasn't necessarily directed at the right thing. Wrinkle mythology is full of misplaced fears and misplaced faith. We treat certain habits like miracle workers and others like poison, often with evidence pointed in the opposite direction. So, instead of guessing what to do and what to avoid, I asked dermatologists to bust some wrinkle myths and misconceptions. (But as the great Oscar Wilde once said, "The truth is rarely pure and never simple.")

Myth #1: Facial expressions are the main cause of wrinkles

Let's address the aforementioned smile-averse situation. If we stop facial movement, whether it's a smile, frown or Elvis-like lip snarl, it would stop wrinkles, right? According to Dr. Behrooz Torkian , a double board-certified facial plastic surgeon based in Beverly Hills, Calif., it's not that simple. Now, some wrinkles really are caused by movement: "A prime example of this is the wrinkles on the forehead, the glabella, or so-called 'elevens,' and the crow's feet," he says. But movement is also competing with bigger forces like sun exposure and collagen loss. His advice is to limit repetitive movement with Botox where it matters, and protect collagen with adequate SPF , a good diet, stress control and no smoking.

To rebuild collagen, Torkian recommends vitamin C , retinoids , growth factors and peptides , along with regular microneedling, radio frequency and laser treatments. And if you happen to have a red light mask in your closet, now's the time to break it out. "Recent scientific evidence on red light therapy has also supported the use of red and near-infrared light to support the metabolic processes of building collagen in the skin," he says.

Myth #2: How much you wrinkle depends solely on genetics

Your bloodline may set things up for your skin, but it doesn't decide the outcome alone. "Genetics matter because your genes shape how thick your skin is, how well you hold onto collagen and how much melanin you have doing built-in sun protection," says Dr. Geeta Yadav, a board-certified dermatologist and founder of Facet Dermatology. This is part of why some people "start creasing in their 30s while others sail into their 60s looking smooth."

However, she points out how identical twins with identical DNA can look years apart in age. She underscores the sun's impact on our skin, which makes movement seem like a minor threat by comparison. "Sun alone is estimated to account for around 80% of the visible aging we see on the face," she says.

Myth #3: The more expensive the moisturizer, the better

By now, you probably know that drugstore beauty can go toe-to-toe with luxury brands , and moisture is no exception. "I have always believed that paying a lot for a moisturizer is not worth it," says Torkian. What matters, he says, is what's actually in the jar. Moisturizers break down into three parts: humectants that draw in water, emollients that soften and occlusives that seal it all in. Beyond that, you want to consider whether it has actives, such as peptides, retinoids, hydroxy acids and niacinamide. "As a general rule, I personally avoid the super expensive and the super cheap," he says.

Myth #4: Dry skin causes wrinkles; oily skin ages better

"One of the most essential factors in the appearance of wrinkles in skin is the hydration of the collagen, hyaluronic acid and elastin within the dermis and epidermis," explains Torkian. Oil definitely supports it, as more sebaceous glands mean the skin has a built-in defense system against losing that moisture. However, dry skin doesn't necessarily mean you're doomed. It just needs that same protection in a different way: "Moisturizers such as ceramides to augment the skin barrier" versus retinoids and hydroxy acids for oily skin — at least as a starting point.

According to Torkian, internal hydration is definitely a part of the picture, but only if the skin barrier is already intact and topical moisture is in place. But water alone doesn't do the plumping. A 2015 study published in Clinical, Cosmetic and Investigational Dermatology showed that adding roughly 2 liters of water a day to women's diets for a month significantly improved skin hydration and biomechanics.

Ultimately, it's less that water plumps wrinkles and more that dehydration accelerates them. Yadav is more blunt, saying that drinking more water is unlikely to meaningfully change wrinkles.

Myth #6: Retinol and tretinoin are interchangeable

Both retinol and tretinoin speed up cell turnover and rebuild collagen, which smooths and softens wrinkles over time. But the real question is which one gets you there and how fast. Torkian breaks down how tretinoin is the active compound itself, whereas retinol has to go through two steps to convert into tretinoin. "This means that using tretinoin can lead to quicker results and quicker onset of the results, but it can also feel a little bit more harsh to skin that has not adjusted to retinoic acid yet," he says. Over the long term, results from both can be very similar, he adds.

Myth #7: Only in-office procedures can reverse wrinkles, not topicals

According to Torkian, the answer to this isn't a flat no. "There are some topicals that can be very helpful in reversing wrinkling," he says, "provided that the wrinkling has not gone out of hand." Retinoids, especially prescription tretinoin, have decades of trial evidence behind them, while vitamin C, growth factors and peptides can also make a difference.

But he doesn't stop there: "Another essential factor is whether proper prevention is being employed at the same time as using the topical that is intended to reverse wrinkling." In other words, a product working solo, without sun protection or consistency, applied to wrinkles that are already deeply set isn't a fair test of what topicals can actually do.

Myth #8: The neck and chest age faster than the face

While it's true that the skin on the neck and chest is very different from the skin on the face (mainly because there are fewer oil glands), Torkian pushes back on the framing of this myth, and points out the impact of our behavior. "One thing to keep in mind about the skin of the neck and chest is that they rarely get any love," he says. "I always like to remind my patients that when they have their skin-care routine, they should not forget the neck and chest. It is natural to want to use all of your expensive skin-care products on what you feel people are looking at the most, but spreading a little love below the chin can be impactful over time in preventing neck and chest aging."

Myth #9: Botox is the best treatment for all kinds of wrinkles

Yadav is clear that Botox is excellent for softening the dynamic lines caused by repeated muscle movement. "Frown lines, forehead lines and crow's feet respond beautifully, because quieting the muscle stops it folding the skin above it thousands of times a day," she explains. But it does much less for lines already etched in when your face is completely at rest, and very little for crepey texture, sun damage or the sagging that comes from lost volume and laxity, she says.

At under $10, this effective cream is proof of Myth #3 — you don't have to splurge to get real results. It pairs retinol with bakuchiol, a plant-derived retinol alternative that helps soften irritation, plus vitamin E and allantoin to keep skin calm. You get softer-looking lines and plumper, less flakey skin without the retinol redness.

One of the most effective anti-aging treatments available without a prescription is Differin. This dermatologist favorite can help improve skin texture, fine lines and overall skin tone as long as you're consistent. It can also help build collagen, which, in turn, makes skin look brighter and bouncier.

This budget-friendly moisturizer does barrier-repair work while you sleep thanks to a powerful trio of ceramides, hyaluronic acid and peptides. It's essentially the ingredient-category cheat sheet from Myth #6 packed into an affordable cream.

Vichy Mineral 89 Booster, Hyaluronic Acid Serum

We voted this the best drugstore face serum for a reason. It contains Vichy's legendary Volcanic Water, which is sourced from French volcanoes and contains 15 essential minerals that strengthen, protect and repair the skin barrier​.

Celimax The Vita-A Retinal Shot Tightening Dual Cream

This Celimax cream features a two-in-one dispenser, releasing a retinal cream with 5% panthenol soothing cream at the same time. It also explicitly treats the neck alongside the face with matrixyl 3000, a peptide complex, for firming, so you can make sure Myth #8 gets covered.

articles.title: Elon Musk Says SpaceX Needs More Power Than New York City in a Heatwave. These 2 Nuclear Stocks Should Benefit.
articles.summary: Artificial intelligence adoption continues to require more energy.
articles.body:
SpaceX (NASDAQ: SPCX) CEO Elon Musk is concerned with the supply of electricity in the U.S. Over the past three months, the space company has spent $15.8 billion scaling its artificial intelligence compute infrastructure -- infrastructure that is highly energy-intensive. During SpaceX's first earnings call on Aug. 11, Musk stressed the need to scale up its energy infrastructure in tandem.

"[O]ur tentative target is to actually have 20 gigawatts at the power and cooling level online by the end of next year," Elon Musk revealed. "Now I don't think we're going to achieve 20 gigawatts, but we want to have a series of projects that cumulatively come to 20 gigawatts by the end of next year. Some of them won't pan out exactly on time, but I would expect that we still probably have at the power plant level, something close to 15 gigawatts."

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

For comparison, New York City requires roughly 10 gigawatts of power during a heatwave, putting SpaceX's near-term energy needs well beyond the largest city in the U.S.

Thus far, SpaceX has relied on a variety of renewable and conventional electricity sources to power its growing data center empire. More recently, it has leaned heavily on natural gas. But in the long term, new solutions that provide large amounts of reliable, low-carbon baseload power will be needed.

It's no wonder, then, that the CEO of OpenAI -- one of SpaceX's biggest competitors -- personally invested in a relatively new approach to nuclear energy. Fortunately for investors, there are two pure-play stocks betting on that exact thesis.

Nuclear energy is perfect for artificial intelligence

In general, nuclear energy is well-suited to meeting the rising energy needs of SpaceX and other AI companies.

"Unlike wind turbines and solar arrays that generate electricity intermittently, nuclear power plants typically put out a constant supply of energy to the grid, which aligns well with what data centers need," observes an industry report by the MIT Technology Review .

The main issue with nuclear is simply how long it takes to get a new plant online. "The problem is how to build up nuclear capacity -- existing facilities are limited, and new technologies will take time to build," the MIT Technology Review warns. "To meet electricity demand from data centers expected in 2030 with nuclear power, we'd need to expand the fleet of reactors in the country by half."

articles.title: United's biggest-ever international expansion includes 10 destinations worth a closer look
articles.summary: The Chicago-based carrier will offer new nonstop flights across Europe and Asia, making places like Marseille, Valencia and Okinawa easier to reach.
articles.body:
Ever wanted to fly nonstop to Slovenia? You're in Luxembourg!

United Airlines on Tuesday announced what the airline says is the largest expansion in its history, with 10 new international destinations — including the first nonstop flights by a U.S. airline to Ljubljana, Slovenia and Luxembourg City — and 13 new routes.

"We've opened up more of the world to our customers," Patrick Quayle, United's senior vice president of global network planning, said on a conference call with reporters . "Next summer, we'll give them more opportunities … to explore places that they may not have previously considered."

Beginning in March 2027 and continuing into the summer, United will launch nonstop service to the following destinations across Europe and Asia:

Luxembourg City, Luxembourg — from Newark

Terceira, Azores, Portugal — from Newark

Toulouse, France — from Washington Dulles

The flights to Ibiza, Valencia, Luxembourg City, Marseille and Toulouse will be aboard United's new Airbus A321XLR. The plane is scheduled to begin flying select domestic routes in September, followed by international service in December.

The Chicago-based carrier has added nearly 60 international destinations to its route map since 2017, and now flies to more than 160 international destinations.

United is also adding new international routes to destinations it already serves from three of its U.S. hubs: daily service from Los Angeles to Osaka, Japan; nonstop service from Washington, D.C., to Milan, Italy; and daily nonstop service from Denver to Paris.

The airline said it will also resume three-times-weekly service from San Francisco to Tel Aviv on March 28, 2027.

Related: Delta just made it easier to fly business class. Here's what to know about booking 'Basic Business'

articles.title: Itâs official: Kerala is now âKeralamâ as Centre notifies name change
articles.summary: KOCHI: The Union home ministry has notified 'Keralam' as the new name of the southern state, with the change coming into effect from Tuesday.In a gaze.
articles.body: KOCHI: The Union home ministry has notified 'Keralam' as the new name of the southern state, with the change coming into effect from Tuesday.In a gazette notification issued on Tuesday, the home ministry said, âIn exercise of the powers conferred by sub-section (2) of Section 1 of the Kerala (Alteration of Name) Act, 2026, the Central government hereby appoints the 25th day of August, 2026, as the date on which the provisions of the said Act shall come into force.âEarlier this month, President Droupadi Murmu gave her assent to a Bill seeking to rename Kerala as Keralam, turning the legislation into law, news agency PTI reported.The Lok Sabha passed the Kerala (Alteration of Name) Bill on August 11, followed by the Rajya Sabha on August 12.In the Rajya Sabha, minister of state for home affairs Nityanand Rai said the Kerala Assembly had passed a resolution in 2024 urging the Centre to introduce legislation to change the state's name to Keralam.âThe Bill provides that the state of Kerala will be known as the state of Keralam, and hence there is a proposal to rename Kerala to Keralam,â he said.The Kerala government had forwarded the state Assembly's resolution on the proposed name change to the Centre in June 2024, PTI reported.Subsequently, President Murmu referred the Bill to the state legislature for its views, following which the Assembly unanimously adopted a resolution agreeing with the Bill.The Kerala (Alteration of Name) Act changes the state's name, along with the necessary amendments to the Constitution and consequential provisions.(With agency inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Kochi | Silver Rate in Kochi | Bank Holidays in Kochi | Public Holidays in KochiStay updated with the latest Kochi news. articles.title: What has happened in Plaid Cymru's's first 100 days in Welsh government?
articles.summary: Plaid ministers say they are making good progress but the opposition say little has been achieved.
articles.body:
Plaid Cymru claimed victory in celebratory scenes on the steps of the Senedd in May, after it inflicted a heavy and historic defeat on Welsh Labour.

Since then, it has been an occasionally rough ride for Rhun ap Iorwerth's minority administration.

After 100 days in charge, Plaid ministers say they have laid the foundations to improve public services, and have already made a "tangible" impact in areas like childcare.

But the government failed to get over its first significant hurdle in the Senedd, when its supplementary budget was rejected by the entire Senedd opposition.

Meanwhile opposition parties claim little has changed since Plaid took charge.

Plaid Cymru formed the first non-Labour Welsh government in May, with the party six seats short of a majority of 49.

It won the election on a platform of challenging Westminster to give Wales more control over its own affairs, a promise of a major programme to boost childcare, and to cut waiting times.

The party set out a plan for the first 100 days ahead of the election, which it said showed how serious it was about governing.

It was criticised at the time as a "plan to have a plan", with the party promising to commission a number of reviews or strategies.

The Welsh government said it had made progress on a number of issues in its first few months, including extending free school meals to more secondary school pupils, a new north-south coach service, and a multi-year funding deal for farmers.

But there's a been a focus on a few big areas over the last few months.

Early on, Plaid came under pressure to spell out how it would deliver its landmark childcare policy, which would see free care expanded over a four-year period.

Currently parents in work or training can get up to 30 hours a week for children aged three or four. Plaid want to expand this so at least 20 hours is available from nine months to four years old.

Opposition parties have repeatedly pressured Plaid ministers for answers as to how this will work, demanding costings and a timetable for how the expanded scheme will work - leading a minister to promise more detail .

There were questions from councils , who said the proposal faced serious challenges because of a lack of resources and staff.

The Welsh government now says that all local authorities are on track to provide 12.5 hours of free child-care to two-year-olds via the Flying Start scheme by next March.

Plaid ministers want to phase the rest of the scheme over time - but until that is spelled out the party will continue to face scrutiny over how it's achieved.

The length of time that patients have to wait in the NHS was a totemic problem faced by the previous Welsh Labour government.

Plaid Cymru was careful not to raise expectation of an immediate improvement, telling the BBC last February that the public would not expect a difference within the first 100 days .

The party promised to get waiting times "down to pre-pandemic levels" within four years. In June, the Health Minister Mabon ap Gwynfor said he would eradicate two-year waits in a matter of months .

The latest figures saw two-year waits drop slightly - by 3% to just under 4,100 pathways - but for the third month in a row the total numbers waiting for treatment has risen.

Government Efficiency Minister Dafydd Trystan Davies said the government was laying "the foundations for success to bring down waiting lists" - pointing to work on surgical hubs and a workforce plan.

Plaid is in a minority in the Senedd and the party is vulnerable to defeats if the opposition votes against it.

That happened a few times before the summer recess, including in a crucial vote on an extra Â£300m in spending to reduce NHS waits and expand childcare.

Labour had demanded Â£100m extra to be spent on children with additional learning needs - and the two sides had failed to come to an agreement.

It was the first time a Welsh government has lost a vote on a supplementary budget - which is in addition to the main budget exercise that happens in the autumn.

Laura McAllister, professor of politics at Cardiff University, said she thought the government had been a little naive.

"If you're in that position of being a minority government, transactional relationships and goodwill between the parties is absolutely fundamental."

Since then, Welsh Labour leader Ken Skates has indicated that he does want a budget deal with Plaid .

The Plaid government faced its first major incident over the summer as a devolved government when a number of wildfires broke out in Wales.

The Welsh government came under scrutiny for its crisis management, because unlike the police, fire services are devolved in Wales.

There was criticism from Reform Wales about the time taken in to bring in the army and aerial support .

A minister said lessons needed to be learned with wildfires more likely in the future due to climate change.

Plaid Cymru wants powers over policing and justice, rail infrastructure and the Crown Estate to be devolved from Westminster to Cardiff.

It promised negotiations with Westminster to do that, but turmoil in London has made making the case tricky.

Ap Iorwerth tried and failed to get a meeting with the previous prime minister, Sir Keir Starmer, although the man now in charge, Andy Burnham, held his first face-to-face meeting with the first minister in July .

Burnham has promised to put devolution front and centre of his government.

But his Welsh Secretary, Stephen Kinnock, has said he is not yet "entirely convinced" by the case for more responsibilities for the Welsh government.

Some at Collier's Adventure Farm in Nelson, Caerphilly, were willing to give the Plaid Cymru government time before rushing to judgement.

Raydean Thomas said: "I think they're finding their feet at the moment. Nothing that they've done has been wrong as far as I can say. I think they're thinking of things in the right way."

Faye Dalgleish-McGee said: "People do rush to have an opinion a bit too quickly - let them get settled in before we start complaining."

Meanwhile, Trish Garner said it was important to wait to see what their plans are.

"But I don't hear an awful lot about what they're going to do and that's my feeling," she added.

Michael Davies said his life had not changed since Plaid had got into power, and that politics was the "same old story" with successive governments blaming each other.

"[They say] it's going to take us x amount of years to put it right and then nothing seems to happen."

Julie Jones, who was also at the coffee morning, said it was too soon to judge ap Iorwerth, but that "he came in all guns blazing".

Dafydd Trystan Davies said that "the initial work has been completed on the 96 actions" in the party's 100-day plan.

He said that in some areas the administration had "put the foundations for success in place".

"But in others, we've made tangible real progress that people will be able to feel already," he said.

The first minister is on leave until the end of the week and was unavailable for interviews ahead of the completion of 100 days in government.

Asked by BBC Wales whether that meant the government was playing down the milestone, Davies said it was him that was responsible for 100-day programme and that ap Iorwerth will issue a "progress report" next week.

Reform accused Plaid of focusing too much on "reviews, committees and plans".

Dan Thomas, Reform's Welsh leader, told BBC Wales that things have "just got worse" since Plaid won the election, with waiting lists having "gone up".

"The first minister said during the election campaign that two-year waits would be eradicated within a matter of months. We're now three months into a Plaid government and we're nowhere near seeing those waits being eradicated."

Ken Skates, leader of Welsh Labour, said there was "quite a contrast" between Plaid Cymru's first 100 days and the start of Andy Burnham's premiership.

"We've seen plans and processes here, discussion, a lot of talk, very little action. In contrast with Andy Burnham, we've seen some really, really big interventions that are going to make a difference to people's lives."

Darren Millar MS, Leader of the Welsh Conservatives in the Senedd, said: "Plaid's first 100 days have been a disappointing series of missed opportunities to turn the page on 27 years of Labour rule in Wales."

Additional reporting by Teleri Glyn Jones

articles.title: Unitree post-IPO slide ignites bubble concerns
articles.summary: The Chinese robot maker’s shares have retreated more than 45% from their debut peak.
articles.body:
Shares in Chinese robot maker Unitree have retreated more than 45% from their debut peak, inflicting pain on retail investors and prompting bubble fears.

"Investors were carried ​away by the technology revolution narrative ," a Beijing asset manager told Reuters.

China's newest corporate star , Unitree's founder has downplayed expectations, saying the firm is " lagging behind " in real-world applications.

A flood of new tech shares hitting the market in Hong Kong and Shanghai has worried investors: Alibaba's record share sale, coupled with the massive IPO plans of memory chipmaker YMTC, caused the industry writ large to take a hit on concerns that more Chinese tech firms will follow, "essentially spreading the cost of AI investment across the public and investors ," one analyst said.
