articles.title: RSPB reports record-breaking Cornish chough numbers
articles.summary: RSPB England says 161 Choughs have been counted - 32 more than the 129 recorded last year.
articles.body:
A record-breaking number of choughs have made their nests around the Cornish coastline this summer proving the breed is in "robust health", a bird conservation charity has said.

RSPB England said 161 choughs had been counted in Cornwall - 32 more than the 129 recorded in 2025 .

The charity said the new birds came from 56 successful breeding pairs meaning the average productivity of a Cornish chough nest was three fledglings.

It said choughs died out in Cornwall in the 1970s but returned in 2001 when three birds believed to be from Ireland landed at Lizard Point and began the rebreeding of the population.

Peter Hall, a National Trust chough monitoring volunteer on the Lizard, is on his 11th year of monitoring the nest sites.

He said he had not foreseen a time when he would be monitoring so many sites and "certainly not having 16 choughlets fledge".

Hall said: "The past two winters we have been blessed with chatterings in excess of 20 chough around the Lizard - a far cry from the solitary single pair we had when I started as part of the then nest protection team in 2016.

"Long may the successful return of this iconic Cornish bird delight myself and others."

The charity said the Lizard was the prime breeding ground for the Cornish chough with 26 chicks, 11 more than 2025, emerging from eight nests on the peninsula.

National Trust volunteer Lydia Allt said 2026 had been "an exceptional one" for choughs on the Lizard and across Cornwall.

She said: "Thanks to a quarter of a century of conservation work, partnership working and the support of local farmers and land managers, we are seeing record numbers ofchough across the area.

"Their remarkable recovery shows what can be achieved when habitats are restored and protected, giving wildlife the space it needs to thrive.

"To see so many choughs successfully breeding and feeding across the Lizard is incredibly encouraging and highlights the importance of continuing to care for this special landscape for future generations."

Andrew Jones, chough conservation officer for the RSPB in Cornwall, said the repopulation work would not be possible without volunteers.

He said: "There has been a huge volunteer effort over the past 25 years to protect and monitor Cornwall's iconic choughs and we're grateful to everyone who has played their part in this conservation success story.

"This year, the RSPB and National Trust have had a team of around 50 dedicated volunteer chough watchers, covering the coastline from the Roseland all the way round to Bude, monitoring the breeding efforts and reporting back so we could collate these fantastic, record-breaking numbers."

articles.title: Chloe Moffat: Dad of woman who took her own life says Treasury failed in its duty of care
articles.summary: Chloe Moffat died last year, after she was told of allegations she had shared sensitive confidential information about colleagues, which she denied.
articles.body:
The father of a civil service employee who took her own life the day after a meeting with her managers has said the lack of support given to her by the Treasury "beggars belief".

Chloe Moffat, 26, a personal assistant to a Treasury director, died on 20 May last year, after she was told of allegations she had shared sensitive confidential information about colleagues, which she denied.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, David Moffat said he did not feel the Treasury had taken responsibility for its part in her death.

He added that her loss was "devastating", and had "torn such a big hole in our lives".

The Treasury said "it will learn the lessons from this tragedy".

On 19 May 2025, Chloe went to what she thought was a routine one-to-one with her line manager, but a more senior manager was also present.

"Chloe's first comment was, 'Oh, this must be serious, there's two of you here'", David told Today's Emma Barnett. "So that's the first time that she was aware of anything [that] might be a to do."

"And then they worked through and put several allegations to her that she'd shared confidential information."

During the meeting, David said she had asked on several occasions if she would lose her job, and if she could have a friend there - both of which were refused.

A coroner found at an inquest earlier in August that the Treasury did not apply written disciplinary policy, which would have made clear that if the allegations against Chloe were proven, the likely penalty was a written warning, not dismissal.

"Even though she asked, they said they could not determine the outcome," David said.

Straight after the meeting, Chloe was locked out of her emails. "That was all part of the shock and awe of it all for Chloe," David said.

The coroner found that the meeting between Chloe and her managers "materially contributed" to her death.

Treasury contributed to woman's death, inquest hears Published 10 August

Treasury contributed to woman's death, inquest hears

David said that "there wasn't any duty of care" shown to Chloe by the Treasury.

"There was no safeguarding, there was no support during or after that meeting, from what we've seen and what we've read", he said.

"It beggars belief that an organisation that is front and central in our government cannot get it right."

Asked whether he felt the Treasury had taken responsibility for its part in her death, he answered: "Not yet".

He added, however, that he and his wife had received a letter on Tuesday from the Treasury's permanent secretary, James Bowler, and that they had also met him last August.

David said while they could not change what happened to Chloe, he wanted "to ensure" that "lessons are learned".

"If something positive can come from this unbearable loss that we're suffering, that's all we look to achieve."

He said he and his wife Anne were unsure if they would be pursuing further action against the Treasury, but that they wanted "redress".

A spokesperson for the Treasury said: "The Treasury's deepest sympathies continue to be with Chloe's friends and family, and the department continues to mourn our colleague.

"We will learn the lessons from this tragedy. We are working urgently to respond to the coroner's findings and we have introduced immediate changes to our guidance, support and wellbeing arrangements.

"Chloe's parents have agreed to meet with us so we can hear their views and update on actions the department is taking."

If you have been affected by any of the issues in this story, help and support is available at BBC Action Line .

articles.title: AI receptionist could not understand me, says Doncaster stroke patient
articles.summary: Judith Butterfield from Doncaster says she could not get past the AI service EMMA.
articles.body:
A woman recovering from a stroke has said she was "upset and frustrated" that an AI reception service at her GP surgery could not understand her, prompting her to register elsewhere.

The ASA surgery at Armthorpe near Doncaster was one of many facilities using a nationwide AI system called EMMA to prevent long wait times on the phone.

Judith Butterfield, 71, said after her stroke she attempted to book a GP appointment five times but could not get past the AI service.

Practice manager Claire Oxley said the EMMA service had been "decommissioned" at Armthorpe and was no longer used at the surgery.

Butterfield originally spent two months at Doncaster Royal Infirmary following a stroke in January.

It primarily affected the strength and mobility down the right side of her body and left her speech fragmented.

The grandmother said that the issues with EMMA were compounded because the AI service asked patients not to use speakerphone.

Butterfield said: "I need to hold the phone in my left hand but I can't use the keypad now with my right hand so what am I supposed to do?

"It's not appropriate as a service to have a robot taking details.

"It should be a more personal thing where you're talking to a person and asking questions.

"There was a point in the conversation where I had to repeat my name and she just couldn't understand me.

"If it's a person they can say, 'could you spell that?' But the call just dropped off. It was very difficult and upsetting."

After growing frustrated with the AI service at Armthorpe, the former HR worker has now registered with the Burns Practice in Doncaster.

"They have very good, friendly, helpful receptionists," she said.

"There's still the wait when you phone up and you're in a queue but you can use a call-back service.

"I was amazed when I spoke to a person."

According to the watchdog Healthwatch, Butterfield's experience is not unique with other Yorkshire patients struggling to be understood by AI reception services.

Oxley said: "I am sorry to hear this patient encountered difficulties and felt the need to move to another surgery.

"I can confirm the AI EMMA service has been decommissioned and the practice are no longer using this system.

"We would welcome the patient back to the surgery and I can assure this lady and others that we have successfully recruited more reception staff to help improve our service to patients."

A spokesperson for QuantumLoopAI, the company behind the system, said: "We are sorry to hear about this patient's experience.

"Nobody should feel they have to change practice to be heard, and with her consent we would welcome the chance to look into what happened and help put it right."

The company said every practice using EMMA could set up "priority routing", allowing patients to go "straight through to the reception team on every call".

articles.title: How drought is changing nature's calendar in the West
articles.summary: From early berries to falling leaves, drought is making parts of the West look like autumn.
articles.body:
Trees shedding leaves, berries ripening weeks early and brown landscapes are giving parts of the West an autumn-like appearance despite it still being August.

Experts warn record-breaking temperatures and prolonged dry weather are having wide-ranging impacts on nature, from wildlife food supplies to the health of the soil beneath our feet.

Wildlife conservationist Steve England said: "Trees should be full of leaf. Instead, they look how they should in November, but we're only in August."

Professor Mark Everard, from the University of the West of England (UWE), said while there are "winners and losers" in nature, it is important to see it as "a highly integrated machine that's breaking down".

Heavy periods study to create world's largest biobank

Supercars seized ahead of wedding after M5 incident

Autistic DJ befriended at festival given 'dream' set

England, who has lived near Stoke Park in Bristol all his life, has also noticed fruit ripening much earlier than normal.

He remembers picking blackberries as a child at the end of the school holidays in August and September, but this year he was out picking in June.

However, some berries are also suffering in the drought. England said rowan berries should be double their current size by now, but many have shrivelled in the dry conditions.

He fears that could have consequences for migratory birds such as fieldfares and redwings, which rely on autumn berries as a food source when they arrive in the UK for winter.

If they're "ripening too quick" and disappearing before the birds arrive it could be a "big problem", he said.

He has also noticed trees dropping their leaves much earlier than usual due to the dry weather.

"They are going into survival mode," he added.

Everard described the heat as a "trend that's getting progressively worse" and compared the landscape of Wiltshire, where he lives, to India and Africa with its "Savannah colours".

But he said the "bigger problem" is what lies under the soil.

During intensively dry and hot periods, activity below ground "basically shuts down" and also soil begins to lose structure, which has "major ramifications for everything we can see above the surface" now and in years to come, added Everard, who is associate professor of ecosystem services at UWE.

Although nature has amazing resilience and is able to adapt to a range of extremes, Everard said the problem is "we've changed those extremes".

Record temperatures and record low rainfall can "break nature's capacities to respond" and the system begins to "disintegrate".

Everard said "nature gives us clues and we should be wise enough to listen to those clues".

Paul Keene, who runs a pick-your-own strawberry farm near Cheltenham in Gloucestershire, has also seen crops ripen much earlier than expected.

He said they normally start picking outside in mid to late June, but this year had their first pick in May, which is "incredibly early and all driven by the heat".

The dry weather has not caused major problems for the farm because it has its own reservoir, which collects water and feeds an automated watering system for the fruit.

At the height of the summer temperatures, strawberries were being watered up to 12 times a day.

It is not just strawberries that have ripened sooner than expected, pumpkins on the farm are already looking Halloween-ready.

In previous years, Keene said they have been "waiting for them to ripen in October" so this is very early and may mean they have to be brought in for storage to make sure they last.

articles.title: Solihull mum's perforated bowel ordeal after scan error
articles.summary: Mum developed sepsis after scan error and now calls for better postnatal care for women.
articles.body:
"No-one should have to go through what I did after having a baby," said Natalie after a harrowing post-birth ordeal.

On 11 January 2023, she welcomed her baby girl into the world by caesarean section at Birmingham's Good Hope Hospital, but the newborn bliss soon turned sour and she was left needing emergency surgery for a perforated bowel.

"I knew something wasn't right after Brooke was born, but it felt like my concerns weren't being taken seriously," the 37-year-old from Solihull said.

A University Hospitals Birmingham spokesperson said the Trust "is committed to providing safe, high-quality care" to all patients and to "learning from when things do not go as expected."

Just days after the birth, she began to suffer severe pain and swelling in her abdomen but says her symptoms were downplayed.

As well as debilitating pain, she also suffered vomiting, which included faecal matter, but on 14 January, doctors misinterpreted her scan as showing temporary slowing of her bowel's movements following surgery, medical negligence lawyers at Irwin Mitchell said.

"My condition got worse over several days. Being told I needed emergency surgery is something I'll never forget. I was frightened I might die," the factory worker added.

Despite raising concerns, her condition deteriorated and she developed sepsis. On 18 January, she underwent emergency surgery, in which part of her bowel was removed and a stoma fitted.

The Trust admitted admitted a breach of duty and that a CT scan carried out four days earlier was incorrectly reported.

Decisions about Natalie's care were based on that error, the Trust has said.

"As legal discussions are ongoing, it would not be appropriate to comment on the detail of the case, however, we are working constructively with [Natalie's] representatives."

The mother, who also has a 15-year-old son, explained: "The impact on my life has been huge and I still live with the effects. I continue to struggle with pain, fatigue and digestive problems. It's affected everything from being able to do daily tasks to how I've been able to care for Brooke and Callum."

Natalie is now campaigning for women to receive better care following childbirth and to ensure their concerns are heard.

She added: "I just want other women to be listened to and for warning signs after birth not to be missed."

Jade Elliott-Archer, of Irwin Mitchell, said: "Our investigations have identified concerning failings in how Natalie's condition was recognised and responded to as her condition worsened.

"While these admissions provide Natalie with answers she deserves, they also highlight serious concerns about the care women can receive after birth."

Natalie has since had further surgery, including reversal of the stoma and treatment for complications including a hernia and ongoing wound problems.

"If my experience helps improve care for even one mum, then it will have been worth it," she said.

articles.title: An Oregon high-school junior remembered feeling lost during her first research internship, so she built a free student-led platform to help other teens find mentors and publish research
articles.summary: US News: For many high-school students, becoming interested in research is easier than figuring out how to actually begin. Finding a mentor, understanding rese.
articles.body: For many high-school students, becoming interested in research is easier than figuring out how to actually begin. Finding a mentor, understanding research methods, and knowing how to publish or share completed work can be difficult without the right guidance. Riya Velhal, an Oregon high-school junior, experienced that uncertainty herself during her first research internship. Instead of allowing that experience to discourage her, she used it as inspiration to create a student-led initiative aimed at helping other students navigate research with greater confidence.According to Velhal's profile on StratScholar, she began her first internship at the start of her sophomore year and remembers feeling âextremely lost.â Her experience eventually inspired her to create StratScholar, a student-led initiative focused on giving young researchers access to mentorship, resources, and opportunities to share their work.A difficult first experienceVelhal's introduction to research did not come with a clear roadmap. During her first internship, she found herself without the resources, support system and community needed to understand how research worked. For a high-school student, that can make an already complicated process feel overwhelming. Research involves more than choosing an interesting topic. Students need to learn how to develop questions, find reliable information, understand existing research and communicate their findings. Without someone to provide direction, it can be difficult to know whether an idea is worth pursuing or what steps should come next.Velhal's own experience made her recognise that the problem could potentially affect other students as well. There could be many students interested in research who simply lacked someone to guide them. That realisation became the starting point for StratScholar.Turning experience into actionRather than viewing her difficult first internship as a setback, Velhal used it to think about how the research experience could be made easier for other teenagers. Her answer was to create a student-led platform where young people could find research opportunities, connect with mentors and develop their research interests.StratScholar is built around the idea that students should not have to rely entirely on existing personal connections to discover research opportunities. The organisation aims to make research experiences more accessible to middle and high-school students. The initiative also emphasises students learning from one another. Instead of presenting research as something available only to students who already understand the academic system, StratScholar seeks to create a community where young researchers can receive guidance while developing their own interests. For Velhal, this mission is closely connected to her own development as a researcher.Her journey into researchAfter her first internship, Velhal continued exploring research independently. Her StratScholar profile notes that she became involved in independent research related to campaign finance, giving her an opportunity to explore a subject in greater depth. That progression is significant because her experience moved from uncertainty to independent exploration. The student who initially felt lost while trying to understand research eventually began working on her own research interests and thinking about how other students could receive better support.It also appears to have shaped the way she views mentorship. Having experienced the difficulty of entering research without enough guidance, Velhal's work with StratScholar focuses on making that initial transition easier for others.A platform for young researchersStratScholar is not simply intended to connect students with research projects. Its broader purpose is to help teenagers develop the skills and confidence needed to participate in research. The organisation provides opportunities intended to help students learn about research while connecting them with mentors and other students. Its focus extends beyond the research process itself, encouraging students to develop communication, presentation and leadership skills alongside their academic work.This matters because completing a research project is only one part of the experience. Students also need to know how to explain their findings and communicate their ideas effectively. For teenagers interested in eventually pursuing academic careers, those skills can be valuable.Making research less intimidatingKnowing where to begin can be one of the biggest challenges for young researchers. A student might have an interesting question but have no idea which expert to contact. Another might complete a project but not know how to present or publish it. Someone else might simply need another student to explain how the research process works.StratScholar is intended to address those early obstacles by bringing resources and mentorship together in one student-focused initiative. The emphasis on accessibility is also important. Research opportunities can sometimes feel out of reach for students who do not already have connections to universities, researchers, or specialised programmes. A platform built specifically for younger students can provide a more approachable entry point.From feeling lost to helping othersVelhal's story ultimately began with a problem she personally encountered. She entered her first research internship excited about the opportunity but found herself unsure about what to do next. Instead of keeping that experience to herself, she turned it into a question: how could other students avoid feeling the same way?That question eventually became StratScholar. Her work demonstrates how a frustrating experience can sometimes lead to a practical solution. By creating a student-led initiative focused on mentorship, research opportunities, and sharing student work, Velhal is attempting to make the research journey more accessible to teenagers who might otherwise struggle to find their way.For young students interested in research, having an idea is often only the beginning. Finding someone who can help turn that idea into meaningful work can make all the difference. StratScholar is Velhal's effort to make that connection easier, and to ensure that fewer students have to feel as lost as she once did.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: SpaceXâs $100 billion bet on Louisiana Starbase: 3,000 jobs, rocket hub - why it matters
articles.summary: US News: SpaceX plans to build a $100 billion, 125,000-acre (50,585-hectare) Starship launch complex on Pecan Island in US' southern Louisiana, an area that se.
articles.body: SpaceX plans to build a $100 billion, 125,000-acre (50,585-hectare) Starship launch complex on Pecan Island in US' southern Louisiana, an area that serves as protected habitat for dozens of migratory bird species and whose receding wetlands help shield inland communities from flooding.The proposed Starbase Louisiana would become SpaceX's fourth US launch site and its second Starbase. Construction is due to begin in 2027, with the first Starship launch targeted for 2029 and thousands of missions annually envisioned over time.SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell presented the plans near the proposed site in Vermilion Parish alongside Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry and other senior state officials, according to Reuters.Exxon settlement cleared way for launch plansSpaceX's arrival follows the end of a roughly decade-long legal battle over wetland loss involving the same coastal area.Local parishes had sued ExxonMobil, alleging that coastal drilling and canal dredging by the oil company contributed to the disappearance of Louisiana wetlands. The state and Exxon agreed to settle the case in June, and a court order shows it was dismissed the following month.The resolution cleared the way for SpaceX's proposed development along an approximately 18-mile (29-km) coastal strip. Louisiana Economic Development Secretary Susan Bourgeois said discussions between the company and the state had been under way since February.Shotwell said extensive parts of the site would remain natural wetland without buildings or other infrastructure. An animated presentation released by SpaceX showed several launch pads separated by large green areas.Site would make fuel and generate powerSpaceX planned the Louisiana facility as a largely self-sustaining launch base rather than a rocket factory.The complex is expected to produce methane for Starship propellant, generate its own electricity and include vehicle-processing facilities. Deep-water shipping infrastructure would allow Starships to be transported from Texas, while Shotwell said the site would probably also have an airport.Unlike SpaceX's Starbase in South Texas, rockets would not be manufactured at this complex.Pecan Island's location also serves SpaceX's satellite plans. Launches heading south across Gulf waters could reach sun-synchronous orbits, whose sunlight conditions are suitable for the solar-powered AI satellites envisioned by Elon Musk.SpaceX targets thousands of Starship missionsThe company eventually wants Starbase Louisiana to handle thousands of Starship missions a year, although reaching that frequency will depend on SpaceX overcoming technical and regulatory obstacles.Starship remains under development. The South Texas Starbase is currently its only active launch site, while SpaceX is constructing two Starship pads in Florida beside Falcon 9 launch infrastructure. The company also flies Falcon 9 missions from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California.Musk sees Starship as central to an expansion of the Starlink satellite network and has proposed eventually deploying as many as one million satellites capable of processing AI workloads in orbit.NASA also plans to use Starship as part of its Artemis programme to return astronauts to the Moon.More than 3,000 jobs plannedSpaceX says Starbase Louisiana would create more than 3,000 jobs in the region.Louisiana's governor's office puts average annual pay for the jobs at $92,600, 192% above the average wage in Vermilion Parish. Landry has backed the project as a source of employment, investment and coastal protection.The development is part of a broader expansion by SpaceX across the southern United States. The company has built Colossus AI data centres in Tennessee and Mississippi and Starlink facilities in Austin, Texas, and is planning a chip plant in central Texas.Texas record puts wildlife impact in focusSpaceX says it will help finance conservation and restoration work while Starbase Louisiana is being built, including efforts to restore Pecan Island's shrinking marshes and coastline.The wetlands perform another role beyond providing wildlife habitat: they act as a buffer against flooding farther inland during periods of heavy rainfall.Shotwell said birds displaced temporarily by launches would return after the rockets had departed.SpaceX's experience at its first Starbase in Boca Chica, Texas, provides a precedent for the environmental debate likely to accompany the Louisiana development. The company transformed Boca Chica into the Starbase company town with support from local officials, while some residents objected over water and environmental concerns, noise and pressure to sell their property.Environmental groups have alleged that Starship launches at the Texas site struck shorebirds and their nests with gravel and debris.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: At least 15 infants are killed in Islamabad hospital fire, local media reports
articles.summary: At least 15 infants were killed when a fire broke out at a state-run hospital in Pakistan‘s capital Islamabad, triggered by a fault in air conditioning systems, local broadcaster Geo TV reported on Wednesday.
articles.body: ISLAMABAD — At least 15 infants were killed when a fire broke out at a state-run hospital in Pakistan’s capital, Islamabad, set off by a fault in air-conditioning systems, local broadcaster Geo TV reported Wednesday. The blaze started around 7 a.m. (10 p.m. Tuesday ET) at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS), on the third floor of the hospital’s mother and child health ward, the broadcaster said. The incident is among the deadliest hospital fires in recent years in the country, where government health care is subsidized but facilities are under-resourced and overburdened while watchdogs have frequently criticized state-run facilities as mismanaged. There were 16 newborns in the ward when the fire broke out, one of whom was rescued, Geo reported. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has directed authorities to conduct an immediate investigation, his office said. “Those responsible should be identified, and the strictest action should be taken,” Sharif’s office said in a statement. The ward was cordoned off and ambulances were seen outside the hospital building, according to a Reuters witness. PIMS, centrally located in Islamabad, is one of the city’s main public hospitals. Jailed former Prime Minister Imran Khan was briefly treated there last week.

articles.title: Your guide to Shrewsbury Folk Festival
articles.summary: The festival takes place from Friday to Monday at the West Midlands Showground in Shrewsbury.
articles.body:
One of the biggest events in the folk music calendar is returning to Shropshire.

Shrewsbury Folk Festival is held at the West Midlands Showground from 28 to 31 August.

Thousands are expected to attend, with musical acts, dancing, workshops and a youth festival on the schedule.

Here is everything to expect from the four-day event.

Gates open for Thursday camping ticket holders from 15:00 to 18:00 BST.

For Friday camping, they open from 07:00.

Day ticket holders can get in from 12:00 on Friday and 09:00 on Saturday, Sunday and Monday.

Attendees should already have received e-tickets.

The festival starts at 15:00 on Friday, finishing at about 00:00.

On Saturday and Sunday, it begins at 12:00 and finishes at 00:45, while on Monday, things kick off at 12:00 and finishes at 18:00.

West Midlands Showground, Berwick Road, Shrewsbury, SY1 2PF

Yes - there is a car park field on site.

Campers get a free car park pass on arrival, while parking for non-campers can be either booked online or paid for by cash or card on the day.

Car parking is available from 12:00 on Friday and is manned by volunteers in the day and patrolled by security at night.

National Express runs coaches into Shrewsbury.

You can also get a bus to and from the site into Shrewsbury on Saturday and Sunday.

They leave the festival site at gate 1 every 15 minutes and will run between 09:00 and 18:00, with the final bus arriving back at the showground at 18:05.

Shrewsbury train station is a 10-15 minute walk away from the showground.

There are no specific areas where you can leave bicycles.

One side of the festival perimeter is a chainlink fence which bicycles can be chained to.

There are five main stages/areas across the four days: Severn, Pengwern, Sabrina, Village and Dance Tent.

Musical acts include names like Andy Fairweather Low & The Low Riders; Fantastic Negrito; Cara Dillon; Dustbowl Revival; and Talisk x Gardener Brothers: Unleashed.

Barbecues are allowed as long as they are constructed properly and are at least 18 inches (45.7cm) off the ground.

Open fires on the grass and disposable barbecues are not allowed.

Organisers say a bucket of water or sand should be kept nearby in case of an emergency.

They should be situated away from tents and caravans and should not be left unattended.

"We are constantly reviewing the situation in light of the weather and recent wildfires and may revise our guidance," organisers said on the event website.

"Look out for updates via email and social media and for signs on site."

Pandemonium! festival for children aged from birth to 11. Includes music, dance, crafts, storytelling, drama in a dedicated zone in the main arena

Refolkus - a space for 11 to 20-year-olds to music, dance, learn circus skills, henna tattooing and more. Located in The Reef

The Siskin Folk Club - a dedicated venue for sing-a-rounds, music sessions, and the festival choir will also host a Sunday morning multi-faith gathering

Workshops, including singing, songwriting, instruments and crafting

Follow BBC Shropshire on BBC Sounds , Facebook , X and Instagram .

articles.title: 'Hijab on their heads, not minds': Owaisi calls Allahabad HC ruling 'attack on Islam'
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: AIMIM president Asaduddin Owaisi on Tuesday criticised the Allahabad High Court's dismissal of a minor student's petition seeking permissio.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: AIMIM president Asaduddin Owaisi on Tuesday criticised the Allahabad High Court's dismissal of a minor student's petition seeking permission to wear a hijab with her prescribed school uniform in Prayagraj. Calling the ruling an "attack on Islam", Owaisi questioned the court's authority to determine what is essential to the religion.Addressing the Jalsa-e-Rahmatul-lil-Alameen gathering at the AIMIM headquarters in Darussalam, Hyderabad, Owaisi said the ruling was inconsistent with the constitutional protections of religious freedom and freedom of expression. He also pointed to the ongoing Sabarimala case before the Supreme Court, where a nine-judge bench is examining questions surrounding essential religious practices.The AIMIM chief said, "A judgment came from the Allahabad high court. A girl was wearing a hijab to school, and the Court ruled that one cannot wear a hijab. I disagree with this High Court judgment; I do not concur with it. The Sabarimala case is already before the Supreme Court, where nine judges are deciding what is essential. Today's verdict violates Articles 25 and 19 of the Indian Constitution. Who are you to decide what is essential to Islam? Girls are wearing hijab on their heads, not on their minds. It is an attack on Islam."The remarks came after a division bench of Justices JJ Munir and Indrajit Shukla dismissed the student's petition challenging the school's refusal to allow her to wear a scarf over her uniform.The court observed that the petitioner had not produced religious scriptures or other material establishing that wearing a scarf was an "essential" part of her religion, such that its absence would affect her faith. It also noted that photographs submitted before the court showed other students from the same religious community attending the school without scarves.The bench held that where a dress code is uniform, non-discriminatory, adopted in good faith and intended to maintain discipline and institutional identity, determining the uniform primarily falls within the school's jurisdiction.The court further said that the student's previous practice of wearing a scarf in lower classes without objection did not create a permanent or enforceable right to require the school to alter its uniform policy. It clarified that the school was not curtailing her freedom of faith but was enforcing institutional discipline, with the uniform forming an essential part of that discipline.The student had completed Class 10 at the same school and sought admission to Class 11. She told the court that she had worn a scarf over her school uniform since Class 6 and that the school had never objected to it.However, when she sought admission to Class 11, the school management informed her that wearing a scarf violated its dress code and refused admission on that ground.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: 'We support protest for accountability': AISA backs CJP's proposed September 5 march
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: The All India Studentsâ Association (AISA) on Wednesday announced its support for the Cockroach Janta Partyâs (CJP) proposed September 5 pr.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The All India Studentsâ Association (AISA) on Wednesday announced its support for the Cockroach Janta Partyâs (CJP) proposed September 5 protest march in Delhi, demanding the withdrawal of FIRs against students and an inquiry into alleged pellet and bullet firing during an earlier march to Parliament on July 20, which was stopped by police."We stand with any democratic, secular, progressive agitation or protest that demands accountability from this government... They must fully withdraw all cases. There should be an inquiry into the firing of pellets and bullets, and the government must be fully prepared to take accountability for the same," AISA president Neha Bora told PTI."From AISA, we are seeing that this is a matter which still remains unresolved. The government itself had committed to withdrawing the cases, but still this is a major issue where students who protested against the government have cases against them," she added.The CJP announced the fresh protest on Monday, accusing the Centre of backtracking on its promise to withdraw FIRs against student protesters. The earlier agitation was called off on July 25 after then Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan stepped down, which had been the protestersâ primary demand.Bora, who was on a 23-day hunger strike in Delhi last month with climate activist Sonam Wangchuk over the NEET paper leak, argued that the protests became necessary because the government had made dialogue with ordinary people difficult.âThe entire point of why students and youth had come out on the streets and why we came out on the streets was that this government has made it impossible for the common people to have a dialogue with them,â she said.Asked about the government's likely response, Bora maintained that a democratic government should engage with people seeking dialogue.âIdeally, the government of a democracy should listen to people who are coming to have a dialogue with it. What will be this government's response is not something I can say,â she stated.On the Delhi Police's statement that it had not received a request for the September 5 march and would review any request, Bora said AISA would await its response.âThere have been many protests in the past without police permission being granted, and we are those people who stand by the democratic principle that protests do not need permission,â she stated.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.body: 'The Times of India' brings you 'Hack of the Day'âa new weekday series of quick, practical solutions to everyday hassles. articles.title: Libyan cleared after Lockerbie bombing trial dies aged 70
articles.summary: A Facebook post by Libyan Airlines announced the death of Al Amin Khalifah Fhimah and expressed the company's condolences to his family.
articles.body:
A Libyan who was cleared after standing trial over the Lockerbie bombing is reported to have died aged 70.

Al Amin Khalifah Fhimah was accused of murdering 270 people in the attack on Pan Am Flight 103 in December 1988.

He was found not guilty but a second Libyan, Abdulbasset Al Megrahi, was convicted of playing a key role in the bombing of the American airliner.

A Facebook post by Libyan Airlines announced his death and expressed the company's condolences to his family.

Fhimah worked for the carrier in Malta before the bombing of Pan Am 103.

The charges against Fhimah and Megrahi were first announced by Scotland and the United States in 1991.

Years of sanctions imposed on Libya by the United Nations led to the two men being handed over to stand trial at a Scottish court sitting in the Netherlands.

In 2001, three judges convicted Megrahi of mass murder and jailed him for life, but found Fhimah not guilty.

Megrahi died from cancer in 2012, after being freed on compassionate grounds by the Scottish government.

Fhimah always denied any involvement and was welcomed home to Libya by the country's late dictator Colonel Muammar Gaddafi.

In 2022, the FBI revealed that he had been implicated in the case again, through an alleged confession made by another Libyan who is facing trial in the United States.

Abu Agila Mohammad Masud Kheir Al-Marimi is said to have told a Libyan police officer that he took part in a plot to bomb the plane along with Fhimah and Megrahi, when all three were members of the Libyan intelligence service.

Al-Marimi has denied making the bomb that brought down the jumbo jet and claims the confession is false and was made under duress.

The contents of Al-Marimi's alleged confession and other new evidence which has emerged from Libya has led to speculation that Fhimah could have faced a second trial over the attack on the airliner.

The indictment against Fhimah announced by the US Government in 1991 is still outstanding.

Under the Double Jeopardy (Scotland) Act 2011 , external , a suspect can be tried over the same crime a second time, if there is new evidence - which was not available during the original trial - that substantially strengthens the case against them.

The BBC understands Scottish and US prosecutors would have looked at taking fresh action against Fhimah, if Al-Marimi was convicted by the court in Washington.

But pursuing a prosecution in Scotland or the US would have been legally challenging and politically sensitive, given his acquittal by the Scottish court in 2001.

Al Marimi is now due to stand trial in Washington in January, after a federal court judge agreed to postpone the case for a third time.

The delay, requested by the defence, followed the emergence of "newly discovered" evidence on the case.

The postponement was not connected to Fhimah's reported death.

articles.title: India vs Sri Lanka 2nd Test, Day 4 live score, weather report, toss, winning probability, result and highlights from Colombo
articles.summary: Track Sri Lanka vs India 2nd Test, full scorecard, updates, and real-time victory chances from the SSC Ground in Colombo.
articles.body:
India vs Sri Lanka 2nd Test, Day 4 live score, weather report, toss, winning probability, result and highlights from Colombo originally appeared on Cricket News . Add Cricket News as a Preferred Source by clicking here .

KEY MATCH DETAILS: (Sri Lanka vs India 2nd Test)

Venue: Galle International Stadium, Galle

Captains: Shubman Gill ( India ), Dhananjaya de Silva ( Sri Lanka )

Toss result: India won the toss and opted to bat.

Live Telecast: Sony Sports Network (India), Willow TV (USA, Canada), Sky Sports (UK, England)

Umpires and match officials: Ahsan Raza, Rod Tucker (On-field umpires), Sharfuddoula (TV Umpire), Raveendra Wimalasiri (Reserve Umpire), Andy Pycroft (Match Referee)

Sri Lanka vs India 2nd Test live match Scorecard

Follow along with the latest live scorecard here as the match unfolds, or click here for key text commentary updates from the action.

Sri Lanka vs India 2nd Test Live 2026 Live Score Updates

Hello everyone, and welcome to the live blog for the Sri Lanka vs India 1st Test in Galle.

Sri Lanka vs India, 2nd Test, Day 4: Live updates and scorecard

Eight wickets needed for India to seal it, while Sri Lanka have to find another 130 runs just to clear the deficit and make the visitors chase. The deck isn't playing any crazy tricks, yet there's enough nip and turn to stop anyone from ever feeling truly set.

For the hosts, it's all about testing Indian stamina. The visitors have already toiled through 111.4 overs across the past two days. Drag this out with a couple of gritty, long-drawn stands, and fatigue could well become a factor.

Pasindu Sooriyabandara has looked in fine touch on 35, while Kamindu Mendis is eager to snap a quiet run and make a statement before the series wraps up. A serious test of character ahead for this batting lineup.

Back in a flash for the post-lunch session!

SL fail to save follow-on! Dinusha is trapped at slips by Rahul off Suthar. India have enforced the follow-on, which means Sri Lanka must come out to bat once again.

Sonal Dinusha scores his second Test century, and Jaiswal is the first Indian to clap while standing in gully. SL still need 21 runs to avoid follow-on.

Sri Lanka vs India, 2nd Test, Day 3: Live updates and scorecard

Stumps: Sri Lanka still have a long way to go

The hosts still need 38 runs needed to avoid the follow-on as Suthar and Krishna ripped through the Sri Lankan batting lineup with three wickets apiece.

Dinusha remains the only man standing between a total collapse with the all-rounder nearing his second century in as many matches.

The hosts have somewhat reduced the margin but they are still 87 runs short of avoiding follow-on.

Pasindu Sooriyabandara misses out on his century as Sri Lanka's collapse continues.

After the setback at the end of Day 2, the hosts show great fight in the first session as they cross the 100-run mark.

The hosts were in trouble at the end of Day 2 of the series decider in Colombo. Sri Lankan batters will hope to bat all through Day 3 to stand a chance of saving the game.

Sri Lanka vs India, 2nd Test, Day 2: Live updates and scorecard

A touch of late drama rounded off a rain-shortened second day. Dhruv Jurel's century carried India past the 500 mark, prompting the declaration. Weather had already eaten up two hours of the morning session, and further showers interrupted Sri Lanka's innings later on.

Once play resumed, Prasidh Krishna and Manav Suthar made quick inroads with a wicket each, leaving the hosts in early trouble at 8/2 before the umpires called time.

Jurel gets his century, and then rain stops play

Jurel took 22 balls to get to his 100 from 99. However, it was worth the wait. It was a gem of an innings, and India declared at 503/9. Sri Lanka come out to bat but bad light stops play.

Rain forces play stoppage as Jurel nears milestone

Stoppage due to rain forced an early tea as Dhruv Jurel nears his sophomore century. Batting at 95, the all-rounder has completely grounded India's innings after a flurry of wickets nearly threatened to end the visitor's play in the second innings.

However, with sheets covering the pitch and rain coming down heavily, he might need to wait a bit more for his milestone.

Pant was finally dismissed, once again missing out on a century while Prabath Jayasuriya quickly sent Manav Suthar back to the dressing room to get Sri Lanka's eighth wicket.

Jurel continues to hold India's innings from one end as the hosts hope to wrap up the visitors within this session.

A blundering partnership between the two tailenders

India is looking to build up towards a big score as the visitors go for lunch at 419/6. Both Pant and Jurel continue to find boundaries as the initial scare of Fernando has made way for quick runs. The Indian wicketkeeper seems particularly eager for a big score after his playing time was cut short on Day 1.

Pant returned to the crease after Jain's dismissal and quickly put the pedal to the metal. The duo bagged their second half-centuries of the series while also helping India breach the 400-run mark.

Fernando gets an early breakthrough for Sri Lanka

The fast bowler bowls it short, forcing Jain to go for a flick landing straight on his left at the gully as Kamil Mishara completes the catch. This is Fernando's fourth wicket as the hosts look to quickly dismiss India.

Sri Lanka vs India, 2nd Test, Day 1: Live updates and scorecard

India ends day 1 with 300 runs on the board

India ends the day with 300 runs on the board with Dhruv Jurel and Saransh Hain on the crease for the guests. Sri Lanka was able to dismiss Jadeja just before stumps, giving Fernando his third wicket of the day.

Keshara Nuwantha has ended Devdutt Padikkal's stay on 117 off 193 balls, a huge wicket for Sri Lanka with the second new ball just around the corner. Pushed through quicker on a flatter trajectory, it was a delivery Padikkal should have come forward to. articles.title: Sugar prices: Why India is importing the sweetener for the first time in nearly a decade
articles.summary: Domestic sugar prices have jumped nearly 40%, forcing India to import 1 million tonnes of the sweetener.
articles.body:
India, the world's largest consumer of sugar, is trying to avoid a bittersweet festive season.

Sugar prices have jumped nearly 40% in the past two months, prompting the government to import 1 million tonnes for the first time in nearly a decade.

The move comes as demand surges from August, with festivals such as Ganesh Chaturthi, Dussehra and Diwali leading into the busy wedding season. Food and beverage companies also begin stocking up for one of their busiest sales periods, adding pressure on wholesale prices.

Production is now expected to be 30.6 million tonnes in the current season, which runs from October 2025 to September 2026 - 11% below the government's earlier estimate of 34.3 million tonnes.

The squeeze has sent prices soaring. A kilo of sugar that cost around 40-45 rupees ($0.42-0.47; £0.31-0.35) in May-June was selling for more than 58-60 rupees in several markets in August, although prices have begun to ease slightly.

But how did a country, which is also the world's second-largest sugar producer, end up needing imports?

The government has blamed lower sugarcane production linked to reduced rainfall during El Niño, hoarding and tighter global supplies after adverse weather hit other major producers.

But experts say another key factor was that India overestimated its own production - and allowed sugar to be exported before the extent of the shortfall became clear.

The government initially approved exports of 1.5 million tonnes this season, adding another 500,000 tonnes in February. Nearly 800,000 tonnes had been shipped before exports were halted in May.

"From allowing exports at the start of the season to ending with an import of a million tonnes is a large variation on production estimates - and that's a big surprise," said Vikram Suryavanshi, a senior analyst at PhillipCapital India.

That matters because India has little sugar to spare. It consumed more than 28 million tonnes last season, not far below what it expects to produce this year.

Nearly three million tonnes is also expected to be diverted to ethanol production, leaving little room for any shortfall.

That is where the imports will help provide a buffer, says Atul Chaturvedi, non-executive director of Shree Renuka Sugars, India's largest sugar refiner and a major ethanol producer.

For three months from 1 September, sugar refineries in special economic zones near ports - which normally import raw sugar, refine it and re-export it - will be allowed to sell duty-free sugar in the domestic market.

The last time India imported sugar for domestic consumption was nearly a decade ago, when the country was grappling with drought.

Other measures are also under way. The Indian Sugar Mills Association (ISMA) has asked mills to begin crushing cane a fortnight earlier than usual to build stocks as the new harvest starts arriving in October.

But that crop, too, faces risks from erratic weather.

Sugarcane is highly water-intensive, and uneven monsoon rains and prolonged dry spells in key growing states such as Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh and Karnataka have affected the crop. Yields are expected to fall, while thinner cane with lower sucrose content means less sugar can be produced.

"Looking at the climate conditions, the next season is also not going to be a bumper crop, although it is too early for actual assessment," Chaturvedi said.

India has frequently restricted agricultural exports when domestic supplies tighten and prices rise. In 2023, for instance, it banned exports of non-basmati white rice for more than a year after crop damage contributed to rising food prices.

But experts say the failure to anticipate the sugar shortfall before allowing exports has raised questions about the government's forecasts.

"This year, the initial projections for sugarcane production did not materialise due to unusual weather in some parts and disease in certain varieties," said Siraj Hussain, a former secretary at the federal agriculture ministry.

The government has not explained why the scale of the shortfall was not identified before exports were halted on 13 May. It has said production fell below estimates because of sugarcane disease and waterlogging caused by excessive rainfall.

The BBC has contacted the agriculture ministry for comment.

Some commentators have also blamed the diversion of sugarcane to ethanol production for the shortage in a deficit year. Even earlier, sugar mills would set aside around 10% of their output for this, helping stabilise prices in times of excess production.

But India making E20, or petrol blended with 20% ethanol, the standard fuel at pumps this year, just as sugar output is low, has added to the challenge, experts say.

The government disputes how much the policy is to blame. It says the share of cane diverted to ethanol has fallen from 12% in 2022-23 to around 9% in 2025-26, and argues that weak production, hoarding and tighter global supplies are behind the sugar price surge.

Some in the industry agree. Deepak Ballani of the Indian Sugar Mills Association (ISMA), which represents private mills producing nearly half of India's sugar, says stocks and monthly quotas for sugar released into the market are comfortable. He argues speculation and hoarding, rather than a genuine shortage, are driving prices higher.

The government has capped stocks held by traders and wholesalers at 400 tonnes for three months to curb hoarding.

Suryavanshi, however, disagrees. India has used such measures before, he says, yet prices continued to climb after the latest restrictions were announced. To him, that points to a real supply squeeze.

And India's decision to import comes as supplies are tightening globally.

El Niño has affected rainfall in Thailand, while heavy rain has disrupted cane harvesting in Brazil, the world's largest sugar producer, where mills are also diverting more cane to ethanol. Heatwaves have battered Europe's sugar beet crop, with France expecting its worst harvest in four years.

US government forecasters expect global production to fall to 184.9 million tonnes this season, from a record 186.1 million tonnes the year before.

London white sugar futures hit $541 a tonne in mid-August, their highest since April 2025, while New York raw sugar futures jumped 4% on the day India announced its imports.

For India, however, sugar availability could improve next year if high prices prompt mills to divert less cane to ethanol.

"At current sugar prices, it simply doesn't make economic sense for mills to divert cane juice to ethanol, so India's sugar scenario should be quite all right going forward," Chaturvedi said.

But the bigger lesson from this year's squeeze, he added, is clear: it is a "warning that going forward, we need to be a lot more careful in estimating our sugar crop numbers".

articles.title: Bristol Water issues first hosepipe ban in decades
articles.summary: Bristol Water says it must protect the River Severn, with the West Country in drought.
articles.body:
A water company has announced its first hosepipe ban caused by drought in more than 50 years, following the lead of other suppliers across the West.

Bristol Water says its "temporary restriction", will come into force from 00:01 BST on Thursday 27 August, to protect water resources in the River Severn.

Wessex Water, Thames Water and South West Water have already introduced bans this summer, with the South West formally declared as being in drought earlier this month.

"Introducing a hosepipe ban is never a decision we take lightly, and we fully appreciate the inconvenience it will cause," said Richard Stanbrook, director for drinking water services at Bristol Water.

Heavy periods study to create world's largest biobank

Why parts of the West look like autumn already

Supercars seized ahead of wedding after M5 incident

This marks the first hosepipe ban in the Bristol Water area caused by drought since 1975, when a dry summer was then followed by 16 months of low rainfall.

However Bristol Water also introduced a short ban in 1990 because of a hole in the bottom of the Gloucester and Sharpness Canal, which then collapsed.

In a statement announcing the latest ban, Bristol Water said although the restriction did not come into force until Thursday, people were being asked to follow the ban immediately.

It includes not using hosepipes for watering gardens, washing cars, patios or boats or filling swimming and paddling pools.

When the weather is as dry as it has been this summer, Bristol Water takes more than half of its supply from river sources, including the Severn via the Gloucester and Sharpness Canal.

However, the Environment Agency and Natural Resources Wales have now applied a drought order to protect the river.

Bristol Water has also pointed to warnings around El Niño, a powerful natural climate phenomenon which pushes up global temperatures and could increase the risks of extreme weather.

Stanbrook said: "After an extended period of exceptionally low rainfall, combined with sustained high demand during the warmer weather, our region's rivers are under significant pressure.

"This is reflected in the Environment Agency's decision to apply for a drought order on the River Severn, where we take a proportion of our water during the summer months.

"The water resources we depend on, particularly the River Severn, support the wildlife, habitats and species that rely on water directly or indirectly, and it's critical we all carefully balance public water use with water needed for our natural environment to thrive.

"We take our responsibility for preserving the water environment very seriously and we know our customers do too. With next year predicted to be the warmest year on record, and with the added pressures from El Niño, we must all think about how we can protect the environment for future years, as well as today."

articles.title: In 1906, Quaker industrialist William Bancroft began buying land outside Wilmington to keep it open for the public; more than a century later, 1,359 acres became the largest unit of First State National Historical Park
articles.summary: US News: In 1906, industrialist William Poole Bancroft began buying land in Delawareâs Brandywine Valley to hold it in reserve for the health and well-being of.
articles.body: In 1906, industrialist William Poole Bancroft began buying land in Delawareâs Brandywine Valley to hold it in reserve for the health and well-being of the public. More than a century later, 1,359 acres of that land became the largest unit of First State National Historical Park.The story of the land, however, began much earlier. National Park service says the Brandywine Valley was originally home to the Lenape people, including the seasonal village of Queonemysing. The village was used for fishing and remained relatively undisturbed while Swedish and Dutch traders focused on the larger waterways in the area.That changed as English colonists, many of them Quakers, began moving further into the interior. Their arrival brought major changes to the valley and affected the Lenape community that had lived there. Over time, European settlement expanded into the area, changing how the land was used and occupied.By the early 18th century, Quaker immigrants had established farms and mills along the creeks. The waterways were important because they provided irrigation for fields, power for mills and routes for transportation. As settlement expanded away from the creek banks, farmers cleared more land and built stone farmhouses.The valley later developed a strong agricultural and industrial character. By the mid-19th century, farmers were cultivating much of the best agricultural land. The area also produced wool, finished cloth, paper and clover seeds. But the water-powered mills that had once played an important role gradually became outdated in the second half of the 19th century.Bancroft begins buying landBy the early 20th century, many of the mills along the Brandywine Creek had stopped operating and fallen into ruin. It was during this period that Bancroft began purchasing property in the valley.Bancroft was an heir to the Bancroft textile mills on the Brandywine. Starting in 1906, he bought land from farmers and small-scale industrialists. His stated purpose was to hold the properties in reserve for the health and well-being of the public.Bancroft eventually acquired more than 1,300 acres. About 1,100 of those acres would later become part of the Brandywine Valley tract of First State National Historical Park.His efforts were not limited to simply buying land. In 1919, he formed the Woodlawn Company. The organisation was later renamed Woodlawn Trustees Inc. Its aims included creating affordable housing and acquiring land for parkland and open space.The land remained privately owned but served as a park for many years. That eventually changed when part of it was transferred to the National Park Service.In 2013, roughly 1,105 acres were donated to the National Park Service. Another 254 acres were donated in 2021. Together, these donations brought the Brandywine Valley unit to 1,359 acres, making it the largest unit of First State National Historical Park.Land becomes national ParkThe land had already been used for recreation before it became part of the National Park Service. In 1959, the Woodlawn Trustees began building bridle paths so their officers and guests could explore more of the area.Some of the paths used existing farm roads, while others were newly created for recreation. By 1968, the paths had been opened to the public. People could use them for hiking, biking and horseback riding.The recreational use of the land has continued under the National Park Service. The Brandywine Valley unit now covers 1,359 acres along the border of Delaware and Pennsylvania.In 2024, the National Park Service completed a Comprehensive Trail Plan for the area. The plan sets out a designated shared-use trail network covering 27.8 miles. The plan includes rerouting, repairing and modifying trails in different parts of the Brandywine Valley unit.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Mattia Perin completes Palermo move
articles.summary: Mattia Perin bids farewell to Juventus. His move to Palermo is now official.Perin first arrived in Turin in the summer of 2018, and from day one, he has alwa...
articles.body:
Mattia Perin bids farewell to Juventus . His move to Palermo is now official.

Perin first arrived in Turin in the summer of 2018, and from day one, he has always given his all for the team - being an example of professionalism, sacrifice, and heart.

In total, he made 71 appearances across all competitions in Bianconero, contributing to the club's success with four trophies: two Serie A titles, one Italian Cup, and one Italian Super Cup.

But beyond the numbers, what truly stood out was his daily commitment, his readiness to support his teammates, and the invaluable presence he brought both on and off the pitch.

Thank you for everything, Mattia. Best of luck for the future!

articles.title: 4 things to watch for Commanders in joint practice with Ravens
articles.summary: Here are four things to watch for Commanders in joint practice with Ravens.
articles.body:
The Washington Commanders headed to Owings Mills, Md., on Tuesday for Wednesday's scheduled joint practice with the Baltimore Ravens . After Saturday's disappointing performance in a 17-13 loss to the Detroit Lions , Wednesday's practice holds more weight than the final preseason game on Friday.

While the final preseason game could determine a few final roster spots for the Commanders, the joint practice with Baltimore is a final opportunity for Washington's starters to get some work against the Ravens' starters. It matters for the Commanders because their starting offense didn't play in the first preseason game and had only three snaps in the loss at Detroit.

What does Washington need to see in Wednesday's practice? Here are four things to watch on Wednesday in Owings Mills.

By all accounts, Daniels has enjoyed an excellent training camp. He looks comfortable in David Blough 's new offense. His accuracy has matched what we saw in his 2024 rookie season. So far, so good, but the Commanders would like to see Daniels have a successful day against the Ravens. Remember, he performed well against the Dolphins in the joint practice two weeks ago, but Baltimore presents a very different challenge. With Daniels unlikely to play in Friday's preseason finale, Wednesday's practice is his final regular-season tuneup. A strong performance against the Ravens from Daniels and the first-team offense would alleviate some of the concerns that arose from Saturday's performance.

This story continues to evolve. It feels like we've been discussing this position since March. Washington still doesn't know what it has in Nick Allegretti at center because he lacks experience there. But the Commanders have repeatedly expressed confidence in the veteran. He will not participate, as he continues to recover from a calf strain that has sidelined him all camp. Washington knows what it has in Julian Good-Jones. He's not a starting-quality player. The Commanders should give rookie Matt Gulbin the entire scrimmage to work with each quarterback, especially Daniels. He needs the reps. It will be interesting to see how Gulbin performs against Baltimore's front seven. This is a big test.

With Washington's starters on the practice field on Wednesday, which receiver will line up as the No. 3 receiver behind Terry McLaurin and Stefon Diggs ? While Blough isn't going to show too much in a practice or preseason game, we'll learn a lot by seeing who gets most of the reps as the third wideout. Luke McCaffrey , Treylon Burks , Antonio Williams , Dyami Brown , Van Jefferson and Jaden Bradley will all get some run, but this could be a test to see who the Commanders trust the most as WR3.

With Will Harris gone, Washington's safety position is set. We know the five the Commanders will keep and have a good idea of their roles. At cornerback, things are less certain. We know Mike Sainristil and Amik Robertson are the top two, with Trey Amos still out. Baltimore's receivers, specifically Zay Flowers , will present a unique challenge for the secondary. How will the Commanders handle Flowers' quickness and his release? Who will have the responsibility of covering Flowers? The corner position remains a concern heading into the regular season with Ahkello Witherspoon 's retirement and Amos' injury. It wouldn't be shocking to see Washington add another cornerback, but this group has another chance to impress against the Ravens.

articles.title: South Korea police find four bodies on Jeju island as missing persons scandal deepens
articles.summary: A police sergeant has been arrested following accusations that he lied to victims' families and prematurely closed missing persons cases.
articles.body:
Four missing people have been found dead on South Korean holiday island Jeju, as local police face mounting public criticism for allegedly mishandling missing persons cases.

Reports emerged last week that authorities were launching a belated search for a woman reported missing months ago. This sparked criticism of the police for failing to search for her earlier.

The scandal has since deepened with the arrest of a police sergeant, surnamed Bu, who is accused of lying to victims' families and prematurely closing missing persons cases.

Four officers in the sergeant's chain of command have been put on administrative leave and on Tuesday President Lee Jae Myung ordered a sweeping reform of the police force.

Since Saturday, police have found four bodies on the island, including that of 37-year-old Jang Mi-ran who had gone missing in May.

On Monday, her body was located at a palm tree farm about 500 metres (547 yards) from where she was staying. She was believed to have killed herself.

Bu is suspected to have closed Jang's case prematurely without confirming her whereabouts.

According to local reports, Bu had allegedly told Jang's boyfriend that he had spoken to Jang over the phone and she had told Bu she did not wish to speak to her boyfriend.

Police also found the body of a man in his 60s from Jeju City on Saturday.

The man had gone missing on 28 June. Bu had closed his case and reportedly told the family that the man was found "safe" but "does not wish to disclose his location to the family".

"We believed the police when they said my father was safe and waited, but after 51 days, what returned was his body," the man's son told reporters.

It is not yet clear whether Bu was involved in the missing persons cases for two other bodies that were found in coastal villages in recent days.

Police are now examining all the missing persons reports that Bu had handled, which number nearly 300.

Jeju is one of South Korea's most popular tourist destinations.

The island, known for its rows of palm trees and sparkling waters, received more than 13 million foreign and domestic visitors last year.

While violent crime is rare in South Korea, suicide rates are among the highest in the world.

Some experts have said the low crime rate is part of the reason why missing persons cases are not taken seriously.

"After experiencing on the field that the absolute majority of missing adults are found quickly, [the officers] tend to assume all cases are like that," Lee Yung-hyeock, a professor specialising in police science at Konkuk University, told Yonhap news agency.

While more than 70,000 adults are reported missing in South Korea each year, 99% of them are marked as resolved within a month.

On Tuesday, President Lee said during a Cabinet meeting that "the recent breakdown in police discipline and irresponsibility in public safety matters have become serious problems".

Pointing out that the police are likely to wield the most power out of all the state's institutions, he said "the Korean people are questioning whether [the police] deserve this large power".

South Korea's national police chief was grilled by lawmakers at an emergency National Assembly hearing on Monday, during which he admitted that "there is a fault in the system".

This scandal comes at a politically sensitive time for South Korea's police.

The government had recently passed reform to transfer full investigative power from the prosecutors to the police, a move they said was intended to curtail the prosecutors' influence in politics.

However, the reform has been unpopular among the public, who have for many years accused the police of corruption and incompetence.

With reporting by Hosu Lee and Leehyun Choi in Seoul

articles.title: 'Be ready for Cockroaches!' CJP doubles down on September 5 protest as 3 demands still 'pending'
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on Wednesday reiterated its plan to hold a march in Delhi on September 5, saying three of the four demands that.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on Wednesday reiterated its plan to hold a march in Delhi on September 5, saying three of the four demands that led it to call off its protest on July 25 were still pending.In a post on X, the party said it had withdrawn the protest a month ago after receiving assurances that all four demands would be met.It said the pending demands were compensation for the families of students, withdrawal of FIRs and no action against student protesters, and an apology from the Rapid Action Force (RAF) and Delhi Police.âEverything will be rememberedâ the party said in its post, while referring to its archive titled âBlack Monday Recordâ, which it said documents the crackdown on protesters, including the use of lathis, tear gas and pellet guns and alleged assaults by unbadged personnel.CJP also said the archive records 11 unanswered questions that it has raised as part of its demand for accountability.âWith each passing day, these questions become harder to ignore and the demand for answers grows stronger,â the party said.CJP plans India Gate to Police HQ march on September 5CJP had announced its September 5 mobilisation earlier, saying the march would begin at India Gate and proceed towards the New Delhi Police Headquarters.The organisation said the march would be led by families of deceased NEET victims and victims of alleged police brutality, with students, youth organisations and young citizens expected to join.CJP had said the decision to resume mobilisation followed a review of the commitments it alleged were made by the government on July 25, after which it withdrew its nationwide student protest.The organisation had also alleged that the government was delaying action on its assurances, particularly on the withdrawal of FIRs against students and protesters.It referred to Supreme Court proceedings in which, according to CJP, the court on August 18 sought a list of FIRs registered across the country so that it could consider dealing with them together.The group had said it withdrew its protest in good faith after talks with Union ministers J P Nadda and Jitendra Singh on July 25. It had then said the government had accepted its demands, including compensation for families of NEET aspirants who died by suicide and withdrawal of FIRs against protesters.The Supreme Court later directed states to release eligible students detained during the protests and barred coercive action against students for the time being.Ranka warns of âCockroachesâ ahead of September 5Responding to Wednesday's CJP post, one of the partyâs spokespersons, Ashutosh Ranka, wrote on X, âWe will not hold back. You might have the govt, the country is ours. Keep your words. Accept our demands. Or this Sept 5, be ready for Cockroaches!âCJP had described the September 5 mobilisation as a peaceful protest march and urged students, youth organisations and young citizens to gather at India Gate.The organisation had earlier led a 37-day protest at Jantar Mantar over the NEET-UG 2026 paper leak, alongside activist Sonam Wangchuk's 26-day hunger strike.On July 25, CJP said it had called off the protest following talks with the government and asked protesters to return home peacefully.Get the latest India News and Live updates.
